Sharp Poincaré interpolation along Wasserstein geodesics

Bang-Xian Han ††thanks: School of Mathematics, Shandong University, Jinan 250100, China. Email: hanbx@sdu.edu.cn    Zhuo-Nan Zhu ††thanks: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China. Email: zhuonanzhu@mail.ustc.edu.cn
Abstract

Let μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} be κ0\kappa_{0}- and κ1\kappa_{1}-strongly log-concave probability measures on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and let (μt)t∈[0,1](\mu_{t})_{t\in[0,1]} be their quadratic Wasserstein geodesic. We prove the sharp Poincaré constant estimate

CP​(μt)≤1−tκ0+tκ1.\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{t})}\leq\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}.

The coefficient is optimal for every t,κ0,κ1t,\kappa_{0},\kappa_{1}, and the result remains valid for extended-valued potentials without symmetry assumptions. Equality at an interior time holds exactly when the two endpoints have Gaussian factors in the same direction, with variances κ0−1\kappa_{0}^{-1} and κ1−1\kappa_{1}^{-1}. All such directions form a maximal linear subspace. This gives an affirmative answer, without symmetry or parity assumptions, to a question of Aishwarya–Rotem.

The proof develops a coupled Bochner method for the two endpoints. We solve a weighted Poisson equation involving the Hessian of the Brenier potential. From its solution we construct a Bochner couple, and separate estimates for its two fields are combined along the interpolation. No curvature bound is needed for the intermediate measures. Applications include centered Gaussian relative entropy, Gaussian Brunn–Minkowski inequalities with barycenter terms, and centered HWI, logarithmic Sobolev, and Talagrand estimates.

Keywords: Poincaré inequality, coupled Bochner method, log-concavity, optimal transport, Wasserstein geodesic, relative entropy, Gaussian Brunn–Minkowski inequality

1 Introduction

1.1 Background and main results

We study whether analytic estimates implied by curvature bounds at two endpoints remain valid along their quadratic Wasserstein geodesic. Convexity of the intermediate measures cannot be assumed: even for uniform measures on convex bodies, the support of a Wasserstein midpoint can be nonconvex [45], and the midpoint is then not log-concave.

Optimal transport has long linked interpolation inequalities, entropy, and curvature. Otto and Villani proved, under curvature hypotheses, the implication from logarithmic Sobolev to Talagrand inequalities and the HWI estimate [44]. Cordero-Erausquin, McCann, and Schmuckenschläger established a Riemannian interpolation inequality through optimal transport [13]. Von Renesse and Sturm characterized lower Ricci curvature by displacement convexity of entropy and equivalent transport and gradient estimates [49]. On Riemannian manifolds with boundary, the first author subsequently proved measure-rigidity results for the corresponding curvature-dimension conditions [26]. These results motivate the study of spectral inequalities along a prescribed Wasserstein geodesic when curvature assumptions are imposed only at its endpoints.

We prove that positive curvature bounds at the endpoints yield a Poincaré estimate along their quadratic Wasserstein geodesic. The sharp estimate is linear in the scale CP​(μ)\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu)}, which is the standard deviation for an isotropic Gaussian. If the endpoint (Bakry–Émery) curvature bounds are κ0\kappa_{0} and κ1\kappa_{1}, then

CP​(μt)≤(1−t)κ0−1/2+tκ1−1/2.\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{t})}\leq(1-t)\kappa_{0}^{-1/2}+t\kappa_{1}^{-1/2}.

Gaussian endpoints attain equality, so the coefficient is optimal. The argument does not require a lower Hessian bound for the intermediate potentials.

The proof links the two endpoint Bochner inequalities through one weighted Poisson equation. It does not propagate convexity of the potentials along the geodesic. The source and target estimates are proved separately. This keeps their sharp constants and is also important for the equality case. We call this argument the coupled Bochner method.

The basic object is a Bochner couple, a pair of vector fields at the two endpoints. The fields have the same divergence datum and are related by D​T=Hess⁡ΦDT=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}, the differential of the Brenier map. Each field satisfies its own Bochner estimate. We first construct this pair from a single scalar Poisson solution. We then interpolate the two fields to obtain the estimate at time tt. We refer to this construction and interpolation as Bochner coupling.

For a probability measure μ∈𝒫⁡(ℝn)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), its Poincaré constant CP​(μ)C_{P}(\mu) is defined as the least C∈[0,∞]C\in[0,\infty] such that

Varμ⁡(f):=∫|f−∫f​𝑑μ|2​𝑑μ≤C​∫|∇f|2​𝑑μ,for every ​f∈Cc∞​(ℝn).\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f):=\int\left|f-\int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu\right|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu\leq C\int|\nabla f|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu,\qquad\text{for every }f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

For integrable functions ff and gg, we use

Covμ⁡(f,g):=∫(f−∫f​𝑑μ)​(g−∫g​𝑑μ)​𝑑μ.\operatorname{Cov}_{\mu}(f,g):=\int\left(f-\int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu\right)\left(g-\int g\,\mathrm{d}\mu\right)\,\mathrm{d}\mu.

If μ\mu has a finite first moment, write its barycenter bμ:=∫x​𝑑μb_{\mu}:=\int x\,\mathrm{d}\mu. If μ\mu has a finite second moment, its covariance matrix is

Cov⁡(μ):=∫(x−bμ)⊗(x−bμ)​𝑑μ.\operatorname{Cov}(\mu):=\int(x-b_{\mu})\otimes(x-b_{\mu})\,\mathrm{d}\mu.

For a random vector XX with law μ\mu, we write Cov⁡(X):=Cov⁡(μ)\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\operatorname{Cov}(\mu).

We write d​μ=e−V​d​x\mathrm{d}\mu=e^{-V}\,\mathrm{d}x for a probability measure, absorbing the normalizing constant into the potential VV. We assume throughout that V:ℝn→(−∞,+∞]V:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(-\infty,+\infty] is proper and lower semicontinuous. We call μ\mu log-concave if VV is convex. For κ>0\kappa>0, we call μ\mu κ\kappa-strongly log-concave if V−κ​|x|22V-\kappa\frac{|x|^{2}}{2} is convex. In the latter case, the classical Brascamp–Lieb inequality [6] yields CP​(μ)≤κ−1C_{P}(\mu)\leq\kappa^{-1}.

Now let μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} be strongly log-concave. Since μ0\mu_{0} is absolutely continuous, Brenier’s theorem [8] provides an optimal transport map TT from μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1}. The constant-speed W2W_{2}-geodesic joining μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} is given by

Ft=(1−t)​I+t​T,μt=(Ft)#​μ0,t∈[0,1].F_{t}=(1-t)I+tT,\qquad\mu_{t}=(F_{t})_{\#}\mu_{0},\qquad t\in[0,1].

Here W2W_{2} denotes the quadratic Wasserstein distance and II is the identity map. The strong log-concavity assumptions give Brascamp–Lieb bounds at the two endpoints, but no corresponding lower Hessian bound for the potential of μt\mu_{t} is available a priori. Thus the Brascamp–Lieb inequality cannot be applied directly at intermediate times.

The following theorem gives the sharp bound for possibly different endpoint curvatures, without any symmetry assumption. For i=0,1i=0,1, let μi\mu_{i} be κi\kappa_{i}-strongly log-concave for some κi>0\kappa_{i}>0. We allow the corresponding potentials to take the value +∞+\infty; in particular, the result includes Gaussian measures conditioned on full-dimensional convex sets.

Theorem 1.1 (Sharp Poincaré interpolation).

For every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], we have

Varμt⁡(f)≤(1−tκ0+tκ1)2​∫|∇f|2​d​μt,for every ​f∈Cc∞​(ℝn).\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_{t}}(f)\leq\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2}\int|\nabla f|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t},\qquad\text{for every }f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). (1.1)

Equivalently,

CP​(μt)≤1−tκ0+tκ1.\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{t})}\leq\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}.
Remark 1.2.

The coefficient in (1.1) is optimal for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and every κ0,κ1>0\kappa_{0},\kappa_{1}>0. Indeed, let μi=N⁡(0,κi−1​I)\mu_{i}=N(0,\kappa_{i}^{-1}I) for i=0,1i=0,1, where N⁡(m,Σ)N(m,\Sigma) denotes the Gaussian law with mean mm and covariance matrix Σ\Sigma. Then T⁡(x)=κ0/κ1​xT(x)=\sqrt{\kappa_{0}/\kappa_{1}}\,x is the unique optimal transport map from μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1}. It follows that

μt=N⁡(0,(1−tκ0+tκ1)2​I).\mu_{t}=N\!\left(0,\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2}I\right).

Thus the coefficient is optimal because CP​(N⁡(0,a2​I))=a2C_{P}(N(0,a^{2}I))=a^{2}.

Remark 1.3.

A stronger statement would replace κi−1/2\kappa_{i}^{-1/2} in Theorem 1.1 by CP​(μi)\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{i})}; that is, it would assert

CP​(μt)≤(1−t)​CP​(μ0)+t​CP​(μ1).\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{t})}\leq(1-t)\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{0})}+t\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{1})}.

This interpolation bound in terms of the endpoint Poincaré constants fails in general, even for strongly log-concave endpoints; see Proposition A.1.

We next characterize equality at an interior time.

Theorem 1.4 (Equality characterization).

Fix t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) and denote mi=∫x​d​μim_{i}=\int x\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}. Then

CP​(μt)=(1−tκ0+tκ1)2C_{P}(\mu_{t})=\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2}

if and only if there exists a unit vector e∈ℝne\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that, under the orthogonal decomposition ℝn=ℝ​e⊕e⟂\mathbb{R}^{n}=\mathbb{R}e\oplus e^{\perp}, the coordinate map 𝒞e​(x)=(e⋅x,Pe⟂​x)\mathcal{C}_{e}(x)=(e\cdot x,P_{e^{\perp}}x) satisfies

(𝒞e)#μi=N(⟨e,mi⟩,κi−1)⊗νi,νi∈𝒫(e⟂)i=0,1.(\mathcal{C}_{e})_{\#}\mu_{i}=N\!\left(\left\langle e,m_{i}\right\rangle,\kappa_{i}^{-1}\right)\otimes\nu_{i},\qquad\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{P}(e^{\perp})\qquad i=0,1. (1.2)

In this case the optimal transport splits along the same decomposition and

CP​(μs)=(1−sκ0+sκ1)2,for every ​s∈[0,1].C_{P}(\mu_{s})=\left(\frac{1-s}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{s}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2},\qquad\text{for every }s\in[0,1].

The restriction t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) is essential in the rigidity statement. At an endpoint, equality constrains only that endpoint and cannot force a Gaussian factor in the other measure. The proof also identifies the maximal subspace of directions along which both endpoints split off the corresponding Gaussian factors; see Proposition 4.2. In [3, Question 1.6], Aishwarya and Rotem asked about the unit Poincaré bound along the optimal Wasserstein interpolation between even 11-strongly log-concave endpoints. Their question was restricted to odd test functions; see also [2, Question 1.4]. Theorem 1.1 proves a stronger result. It requires neither symmetry of the endpoints nor a parity assumption on the test function. Aishwarya and Rotem proved their formulation in dimension one [3, Theorem 4.11], for two Gaussian endpoints, and when one endpoint is the standard Gaussian [3, Proposition 4.12].

Aishwarya and Li used the common-source coupling (T0​(Z),T1​(Z))(T_{0}(Z),T_{1}(Z)), where ZZ is standard Gaussian and TiT_{i} is the Brenier map from the Gaussian measure to the ii-th endpoint. Every interpolant ((1−t)​T0+t​T1)​(Z)((1-t)T_{0}+tT_{1})(Z) is a 11-Lipschitz image of ZZ and therefore satisfies the full Poincaré inequality with constant 11 [2, Remark 1]. This coupling is generally not optimal between the two prescribed endpoints. To the best of our knowledge, the full Poincaré bound for the quadratic optimal coupling of the prescribed endpoints had remained open. Theorem 1.1 proves it along the quadratic Wasserstein geodesic between the prescribed endpoints.

The full Poincaré estimate also controls the fluctuation of the velocity gradient in the second variation of Gaussian relative entropy. We first remove the translation component determined by the means and then apply the estimate componentwise. Let γ\gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For a probability measure μ\mu, define its relative entropy with respect to γ\gamma by

Entγ⁡(μ)=∫ρ​log⁡ρ​𝑑γif ​𝑑μ=ρ​𝑑γ,\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu)=\int\rho\log\rho\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\quad\text{if }\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\rho\,\mathrm{d}\gamma,

with the convention 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0, and set Entγ⁡(μ)=+∞\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu)=+\infty otherwise. Define

𝒟⁡(μ)=Entγ⁡(μ)−12​|bμ|2.\mathcal{D}(\mu)=\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu)-\frac{1}{2}|b_{\mu}|^{2}.

Thus 𝒟⁡(μ)\mathcal{D}(\mu) is the centered Gaussian relative entropy of μ\mu; equivalently, it is the Gaussian relative entropy of the centered translate of μ\mu. For two measures, define

Wc2=W22​(μ0,μ1)−|bμ1−bμ0|2.W_{\rm c}^{2}=W_{2}^{2}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1})-|b_{\mu_{1}}-b_{\mu_{0}}|^{2}.
Theorem 1.5 (Centered Gaussian relative entropy).

Let μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} be 11-strongly log-concave, and let (μt)0≤t≤1(\mu_{t})_{0\leq t\leq 1} be their quadratic Wasserstein geodesic. Then 0≤Wc2≤2​n0\leq W_{\rm c}^{2}\leq 2n, and 𝒟t=𝒟⁡(μt)\mathcal{D}_{t}=\mathcal{D}(\mu_{t}) satisfies the following distortion inequality along the whole geodesic:

e−𝒟t/n≥sin⁡((1−t)​ω)sin⁡ωe−𝒟0/n+sin⁡(t​ω)sin⁡ωe−𝒟1/n,ω=2nWc.e^{-\mathcal{D}_{t}/n}\geq\frac{\sin((1-t)\omega)}{\sin\omega}e^{-\mathcal{D}_{0}/n}+\frac{\sin(t\omega)}{\sin\omega}e^{-\mathcal{D}_{1}/n},\qquad\omega=\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}\,W_{\rm c}. (1.3)

The sine quotients are understood by continuity when ω=0\omega=0, in which case they equal 1−t1-t and tt, respectively. Moreover, equality in (1.3) at some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) holds if and only if μ1\mu_{1} is a translate of μ0\mu_{0}. In this case, equality holds for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1].

In particular, if the endpoints have the same barycenter, then the same statements hold with Entγ⁡(μt)\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu_{t}) in place of 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} and with W2​(μ0,μ1)W_{2}(\mu_{0},\mu_{1}) in place of WcW_{\rm c}. In this case, equality at an interior time holds if and only if μ0=μ1\mu_{0}=\mu_{1}.

Infinitesimal form.

Under the smooth two-sided Hessian hypotheses of Section 2, the proof first establishes

𝒟t′′≥2​Wc2+1n​(𝒟t′)2.\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\prime\prime}\geq 2W_{\rm c}^{2}+\frac{1}{n}(\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\prime})^{2}. (1.4)

This is the differential form of the (2,n)(2,n)-convexity estimate; the finite-time inequality (1.3) follows by a one-dimensional comparison argument and then by regularization.

When the endpoints have the same barycenter, Theorem 1.5 establishes (2,n)(2,n)-convexity along the Wasserstein geodesic for arbitrary 11-strongly log-concave measures. Aishwarya and Rotem obtained the same differential estimate under a pathwise odd Poincaré assumption [3, Theorem 4.6] and verified this assumption in dimension one and along two further classes of geodesics [3, Theorem 4.11 and Proposition 4.12]. For even endpoints, Aishwarya and Li obtained an entropy inequality with sine coefficients along the interpolation of the two Brenier maps transporting the standard Gaussian measure to the respective endpoints. They also characterized equality in the resulting affine inequality [2, Theorem 1.5 and Remark 1]. The present theorem requires neither symmetry nor a pathwise odd Poincaré assumption. It proves the inequality with sine coefficients along the quadratic Wasserstein geodesic and characterizes equality.

Theorem 1.5 also yields a Gaussian Brunn–Minkowski inequality. Gardner and Zvavitch conjectured the dimensional Gaussian Brunn–Minkowski inequality for convex bodies containing the origin [25]. Nayar and Tkocz disproved this conjecture in the nonsymmetric case, even under the assumption that both bodies contain the origin, and proposed its origin-symmetric form [43]. Following important local work of Kolesnikov and Livshyts [37], the origin-symmetric conjecture was proved by Eskenazis and Moschidis [22]. Corollary 1.6 replaces origin symmetry by the assumption that the conditioned Gaussian measures have the same barycenter. Without this assumption, it gives an inequality with explicit barycenter terms. For a convex Borel set KK with γ⁡(K)>0\gamma(K)>0, denote

γK​(A)=γ⁡(A∩K)γ⁡(K)andbK=∫x​d​γK​(x),\gamma_{K}(A)=\frac{\gamma(A\cap K)}{\gamma(K)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad b_{K}=\int x\,\mathrm{d}\gamma_{K}(x),

the Gaussian measure conditioned on KK and its barycenter, respectively.

Corollary 1.6 (Gaussian Brunn–Minkowski with barycenter terms).

Let K0,K1⊂ℝnK_{0},K_{1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be convex Borel sets with γ⁡(Ki)>0\gamma(K_{i})>0. For every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], set Kt=(1−t)​K0+t​K1K_{t}=(1-t)K_{0}+tK_{1} and bt=(1−t)​bK0+t​bK1b_{t}=(1-t)b_{K_{0}}+tb_{K_{1}}. Then

e|bt|2/(2​n)​γ​(Kt)1/n≥(1−t)​e|bK0|2/(2​n)​γ​(K0)1/n+t​e|bK1|2/(2​n)​γ​(K1)1/n.e^{|b_{t}|^{2}/(2n)}\gamma(K_{t})^{1/n}\geq(1-t)e^{|b_{K_{0}}|^{2}/(2n)}\gamma(K_{0})^{1/n}+te^{|b_{K_{1}}|^{2}/(2n)}\gamma(K_{1})^{1/n}. (1.5)

Moreover, equality in (1.5) at some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) holds if and only if K¯0=K¯1\bar{K}_{0}=\bar{K}_{1}. In this case, equality holds for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1].

In particular, if bK0=bK1b_{K_{0}}=b_{K_{1}}, then

γ​(Kt)1/n≥(1−t)​γ​(K0)1/n+t​γ​(K1)1/n.\gamma(K_{t})^{1/n}\geq(1-t)\gamma(K_{0})^{1/n}+t\gamma(K_{1})^{1/n}.

The condition bK0=bK1b_{K_{0}}=b_{K_{1}} does not require symmetry. For example, a regular simplex centered at the origin is invariant under its full symmetry group. It follows that the Gaussian measure conditioned on the simplex has barycenter zero. The simplex is not centrally symmetric when n≥2n\geq 2. Section 5 gives a functional version. It extends the Gaussian Borell–Brascamp–Lieb inequality of Aishwarya and Li beyond even log-concave functions. The new assumption is that the probability measures proportional to f​d​γf\,\mathrm{d}\gamma and g​d​γg\,\mathrm{d}\gamma have the same barycenter. We also provide HWI, logarithmic Sobolev, Talagrand, and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck estimates after centering.

1.2 Proof strategy: coupled endpoint Bochner estimates

The Bochner identity is used only at μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1}. We construct one vector field at each endpoint and interpolate these fields. Thus no curvature estimate is required for the potential of the intermediate measure. Treating the endpoints separately gives the optimal coefficient and makes the equality case accessible.

Step 1: the weighted Poisson equation.

We first work in the smooth setting. Let T=∇ΦT=\nabla\Phi be the Brenier map and set H=Hess⁡ΦH=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}. For a centered function g∈L2​(μ0)g\in L^{2}(\mu_{0}), we solve

−divμ0(H−1∇u)=g-\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{0}}(H^{-1}\nabla u)=g

and define

X=H−1∇u,Y∘T=∇u.X=H^{-1}\nabla u,\qquad Y\circ T=\nabla u.

The same scalar function uu defines both fields, while HH relates them through Y∘T=H​XY\circ T=HX. Smooth approximations of (X,Y)(X,Y) are Bochner couples in the sense of Definition 2.3. A change-of-variables identity for weighted divergence shows that the two fields have the same divergence datum.

Step 2: Bochner estimates at the two endpoints.

At the source, differentiating H​X=∇uHX=\nabla u and using the symmetry of the third derivatives of Φ\Phi shows that

H​D​Xis symmetric.H\,DX\quad\text{is symmetric}.

At the target, the chain rule gives

((D​Y)∘T)​H=Hess⁡u,((DY)\circ T)H=\operatorname{Hess}{u},

so this matrix is also symmetric. Because HH is positive definite, each identity makes the corresponding trace term in the vector Bochner formula nonnegative. Applying that formula at the two endpoints gives

‖X‖L2​(μ0)≤κ0−1/2‖g‖L2​(μ0),‖Y‖L2​(μ1)≤κ1−1/2‖g‖L2​(μ0).\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}\leq\kappa_{0}^{-1/2}\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})},\qquad\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{1})}\leq\kappa_{1}^{-1/2}\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}.

Both estimates are sharp. We keep them separate until the final interpolation step.

Step 3: interpolation of the two fields.

Let Ft=(1−t)​I+t​TF_{t}=(1-t)I+tT and define qtq_{t} on μt\mu_{t} by

qt∘Ft=(1−t)​X+t⁡(Y∘T).q_{t}\circ F_{t}=(1-t)X+t(Y\circ T).

The same change-of-variables formula for weighted divergence yields

−(divμtqt)∘Ft=g.-(\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{t}}q_{t})\circ F_{t}=g.

The separate endpoint estimates imply

‖qt‖L2​(μt)≤(1−tκ0+tκ1)​‖g‖L2​(μ0).\left\lVert q_{t}\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{t})}\leq\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}.

Taking g=(f−∫f​d​μt)∘Ftg=(f-\int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t})\circ F_{t} and integrating by parts proves (1.1) in the smooth setting. The general case follows by regularization and stability of optimal transport.

This interpolation of the Bochner couple is the coupling step. The endpoint norms combine linearly before the final Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. This gives the sharp coefficient.

For the equality case, take a sequence that approaches equality in the Poincaré estimate. The two endpoint estimates and the triangle inequality must then become asymptotically sharp. The associated scalar functions converge to affine functions in the same direction at both endpoints. Gaussian integration by parts gives the common Gaussian factorization. When κ0=κ1=1\kappa_{0}=\kappa_{1}=1, the full Poincaré inequality also gives a Γ2\Gamma_{2} estimate after the translation component is removed. The entropy inequality follows from the standard variation formulas and a one-dimensional ODE comparison.

1.3 Relations to other methods and further directions

Poisson equations, Stein’s method, and isoperimetry.

The construction also has a Stein interpretation. For a probability measure d​μ=e−V​d​x\mathrm{d}\mu=e^{-V}\,\mathrm{d}x, the weighted divergence −divμ-\operatorname{div}_{\mu} is a vector-valued Stein operator. Given a centered test function hh, one seeks a field qq satisfying

−divμ⁡q=h-\operatorname{div}_{\mu}q=h

and estimates its size or regularity. Such estimates are called Stein-factor bounds. Courtade, Fathi, and Pananjady constructed Stein kernels by a variational argument under a Poincaré inequality [15]. Mijoule, Raič, Reinert, and Swan introduced weak Stein equations and obtained weak Stein-factor bounds from a Poincaré inequality [42]. Fathi gave a different construction of Stein kernels through moment maps [24]. In this terminology, CP​(μ)\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu)} is the optimal L2L^{2} norm of a right inverse of −divμ-\operatorname{div}_{\mu} on centered functions. Our field qtq_{t} is an L2L^{2} Stein solution for μt\mu_{t}. In the usual application, Stein’s method compares a measure with a reference law. Here one Poisson solution gives compatible fields at two prescribed endpoints. Their Bochner estimates control the L2L^{2} norm of the interpolated field.

Jiang and Koskela used Poisson equations to derive local isoperimetric and Sobolev inequalities on metric measure spaces from estimates for the Cheeger–Poisson equation [29]. In particular, an estimate of the form

‖∇u‖Lloc∞≲‖g‖LlocQ,1,Δ​u=g,\left\lVert\nabla u\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}}\lesssim\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{Q,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}},\qquad\Delta u=g,

combined with integration by parts and the dual characterization of perimeter yields the isoperimetric inequality with the optimal exponent. Jiang, Koskela, and Yang later obtained local isoperimetric inequalities from Lipschitz regularity of Cheeger-harmonic functions [30]. Their argument uses an L∞L^{\infty} gradient estimate to control perimeter. Our argument instead uses sharp L2L^{2} estimates for two vector fields, one at each endpoint, to control variance at the intermediate measure.

Hessian metrics induced by optimal transport and related flows.

Kolesnikov associates with the Brenier map T=∇ΦT=\nabla\Phi the Hessian metric g=Hess⁡Φg=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}. Its weighted Laplacian is

LΦ=divμ0((HessΦ)−1∇),L_{\Phi}=\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{0}}\bigl((\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi})^{-1}\nabla\bigr),

and the source–target integration-by-parts identity used below is stated in [36, Lemma 2.1 and (2.5)]. Klartag used a dual Bochner formula in his moment-map proof of Poincaré inequalities [32]. Kolesnikov and Milman derived Poincaré and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities by choosing Riemannian metrics adapted to the measure, including Hessian metrics arising from optimal transport [38].

Klartag and Putterman proved monotonicity of the Poincaré constant under Gaussian convolution, using a time-dependent diffusion in one proof and a contracting transport in another [34]. Serres studied the Poincaré constant along the Polchinski flow by dynamic Γ\Gamma-calculus [47]. Those papers concern paths generated by the respective flows. Here the path is a prescribed displacement interpolation, while the Bochner estimates are taken at the two endpoints and linked by the differential of the Brenier map.

Our argument does not use a curvature bound for the Hessian metric. For X=H−1∇uX=H^{-1}\nabla u and Y∘T=∇uY\circ T=\nabla u, the two matrix identities in Step 2 allow the Euclidean vector Bochner identity to be applied separately at the source and the target. They give

κ0​‖X‖L2​(μ0)2≤‖g‖L2​(μ0)2,κ1​‖Y‖L2​(μ1)2≤‖g‖L2​(μ0)2.\kappa_{0}\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}^{2}\leq\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}^{2},\qquad\kappa_{1}\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{1})}^{2}\leq\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}^{2}.

Combining the two separate estimates only at the final interpolation step gives the optimal coefficient in Theorem 1.1. It also allows us to analyze equality at both endpoints.

The matrix fact used to control tr⁡((D​X)2)\operatorname{tr}((DX)^{2}) is the following: if HH is positive definite and H​D​XHDX is symmetric, then D​XDX is similar to a symmetric matrix and tr⁡((D​X)2)≥0\operatorname{tr}((DX)^{2})\geq 0. The same conjugation appears in [33, proof of Lemma 3.1]; a related trace inequality for differentials of common-source Brenier interpolants appears in [2, proof of Theorem 1.5]. Cheng and Zhou proved that equality in the Bakry–Émery spectral-gap bound on a complete weighted manifold forces a Gaussian factor [10, Theorem 2]. Quantitative Euclidean stability was developed by De Philippis and Figalli [16, Section 4] and by Courtade and Fathi [14]. Here equality at one interior time forces both endpoint deficits to vanish and selects the same Gaussian direction at the two endpoints.

The entropy application builds on the second-variation argument of Aishwarya and Rotem [3, Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 4.6], formulated for even measures and even velocity potentials. Aishwarya and Li [2, Theorems 1.5 and 1.7] obtained an entropy-power inequality and a Gaussian Borell–Brascamp–Lieb inequality using a coupling constructed from a common Gaussian source. Unlike that construction, our entropy inequality is evaluated along the Wasserstein geodesic between the prescribed endpoints. Bolley, Gentil, and Guillin derived dimensional refinements of logarithmic Sobolev, Talagrand, and Brascamp–Lieb inequalities [4]. Eskenazis and Shenfeld developed intrinsic dimensional functional inequalities on model spaces [23].

Cordero-Erausquin and Eskenazis proved a functional dimensional Brunn–Minkowski inequality for rotationally invariant log-concave measures [11]. Malliaris, Melbourne, Roberto, and Roysdon obtained Gaussian Borell–Brascamp–Lieb inequalities through functional liftings of restricted geometric inequalities [40]. Our extension instead assumes that the probability measures proportional to f​d​γf\,\mathrm{d}\gamma and g​d​γg\,\mathrm{d}\gamma have the same barycenter. It is proved along the prescribed optimal transport interpolation. Kolesnikov and Milman derived a weighted Brunn–Minkowski inequality from a boundary Poincaré inequality along a geometric evolution [39]. Eskenazis, Giannopoulos, and Tziotziou proved a dimensional Brunn–Minkowski inequality for log-concave measures by a diffusion argument [21].

Wasserstein barycenters.

We next ask whether Theorem 1.1 extends from two endpoints to Wasserstein barycenters. Let λ1,…,λN>0\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{N}>0 with ∑i=1Nλi=1\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lambda_{i}=1, and let μ¯\bar{\mu} be a minimizer of

ν⟼∑i=1Nλi​W22​(ν,μi).\nu\longmapsto\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lambda_{i}W_{2}^{2}(\nu,\mu_{i}).

For N=2N=2, this reduces to a point on the Wasserstein geodesic, and Theorem 1.1 suggests the following question; see [1] for existence and basic properties of quadratic Wasserstein barycenters.

Question 1.7 (Wasserstein barycenter version).

Suppose that μi\mu_{i} is κi\kappa_{i}-strongly log-concave for i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N. Does their quadratic Wasserstein barycenter satisfy

CP​(μ¯)≤∑i=1Nλiκi​?\sqrt{C_{P}(\bar{\mu})}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\sqrt{\kappa_{i}}}\,?

Can one also characterize equality by Gaussian factors in a common direction, with variances κi−1\kappa_{i}^{-1} for the respective input measures?

For two endpoints, the Hessian of one Brenier potential and one scalar Poisson equation produce a Bochner couple. With more than two endpoints, one would need compatible vector fields for several optimal transport maps and their Hessians. It is not clear how one Poisson equation could provide all the required estimates. We leave Question 1.7 open. Han and Liu proved that the Wasserstein Jensen inequality for Boltzmann entropy at barycenters of arbitrary finite families characterizes finite-dimensional normed spaces whose norm is induced by an inner product [27].

Riemannian version.

In a companion work in preparation, entitled Bochner Couples for Optimal Transport on Riemannian Manifolds, the authors study the Riemannian analogue. There Jacobi fields describe the differential of the transport maps in place of the Euclidean identity D​T=Hess⁡ΦDT=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}. A Codazzi-type tensor measures the failure of the matrix symmetry used here. No result from that preprint is used in the present paper.

Organization of the paper.

Section 2 constructs a Bochner couple from a weighted Poisson equation and proves the interpolation estimate under smooth uniform regularity assumptions. Section 3 develops a curvature-preserving regularization and removes those auxiliary assumptions by stability of optimal transport. Section 4 proves the equality characterization and identifies the maximal common Gaussian factor of the endpoints. Section 5 applies the main theorem to centered Gaussian relative entropy, Gaussian Brunn–Minkowski inequalities with barycenter terms, and Gaussian functional inequalities after centering.

We thank Heng Zhang, Shuhao Zhang, and Chiyu Zhou for helpful discussions.

2 Bochner couples from a weighted Poisson equation

We first prove the estimate under auxiliary uniform regularity assumptions on the optimal transport map. A weighted Poisson equation involving the Hessian of the Brenier potential produces a Bochner couple. Proposition 2.5 interpolates its two fields. Smoothness of the endpoint potentials alone does not imply that the Brenier map is a smooth global diffeomorphism. The regularized potentials in Section 3 satisfy two-sided uniform Hessian bounds. Caffarelli’s contraction theory then gives global bi-Lipschitz control. The regularity theorem of Cordero-Erausquin and Figalli for unbounded supports gives smoothness. The statement used in Lemma 3.3 follows directly from [35, Theorem 2.2] and [12, Remark 4 and Corollary 5].

Throughout this section, assume that V0,V1V_{0},V_{1} are smooth and that d​μi=e−Vi​d​x\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}=e^{-V_{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x with Hess⁡Vi⪰κi​I\operatorname{Hess}{V_{i}}\succeq\kappa_{i}I. Assume also that the Brenier map T=∇ΦT=\nabla\Phi from μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1} is a smooth diffeomorphism. Finally, assume that H=Hess⁡ΦH=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi} and H−1H^{-1} are bounded in global operator norm. Equivalently, λ​I⪯H⪯Λ​I\lambda I\preceq H\preceq\Lambda I for some 0<λ≤Λ<∞0<\lambda\leq\Lambda<\infty. These are temporary hypotheses for the smooth argument and will be obtained from the regularization in Section 3. For symmetric matrices, A⪯BA\preceq B means that B−AB-A is positive semidefinite, and ‖A‖HS\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}} denotes the Hilbert–Schmidt norm.

For d​μ=e−V​d​x\mathrm{d}\mu=e^{-V}\,\mathrm{d}x, the weighted divergence with respect to μ\mu is defined through integration by parts and is given by

divμ⁡X=div⁡X−⟨∇V,X⟩.\operatorname{div}_{\mu}X=\operatorname{div}X-\left\langle\nabla V,X\right\rangle. (2.1)

We use the convention (D​X)i​j=∂jXi(DX)_{ij}=\partial_{j}X_{i}.

Lemma 2.1 (Weighted vector Bochner identity).

For every X∈Cc∞​(ℝn,ℝn)X\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n};\mathbb{R}^{n}),

∫(divμ⁡X)2​𝑑μ=∫{tr⁡((D​X)2)+Hess⁡V⁡[X,X]}​𝑑μ.\int(\operatorname{div}_{\mu}X)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\int\left\{\operatorname{tr}((DX)^{2})+\operatorname{Hess}{V}[X,X]\right\}\,\mathrm{d}\mu. (2.2)
Proof.

The weighted integration by parts yields

∫(divμX)2dμ=−∫Xj∂j(divμX)dμ,\int(\operatorname{div}_{\mu}X)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu=-\int X_{j}\partial_{j}(\operatorname{div}_{\mu}X)\,\mathrm{d}\mu, (2.3)

where repeated indices are summed. Expanding the derivative then implies

∫(divμ⁡X)2​𝑑μ=−∫Xj∂i∂jXidμ+∫Vi​jXiXjdμ+∫ViXj∂jXidμ.\begin{split}\int(\operatorname{div}_{\mu}X)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu&=-\int X_{j}\partial_{i}\partial_{j}X_{i}\,\mathrm{d}\mu+\int V_{ij}X_{i}X_{j}\,\mathrm{d}\mu+\int V_{i}X_{j}\partial_{j}X_{i}\,\mathrm{d}\mu.\end{split} (2.4)

Integrating the first term by parts in the ii-th coordinate implies

−∫Xj∂i(∂jXi)dμ=∫(∂iXj−ViXj)∂jXidμ.-\int X_{j}\partial_{i}(\partial_{j}X_{i})\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\int(\partial_{i}X_{j}-V_{i}X_{j})\partial_{j}X_{i}\,\mathrm{d}\mu. (2.5)

Combining (2.4) and (2.5) then yields (2.2). ∎

Remark 2.2.

The first term in (2.2) is not, in general, the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of D​XDX:

tr⁡((D​X)2)=∑i,j∂jXi​∂iXj,‖D​X‖HS2=∑i,j(∂jXi)2.\operatorname{tr}((DX)^{2})=\sum_{i,j}\partial_{j}X_{i}\,\partial_{i}X_{j},\qquad\left\lVert DX\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}=\sum_{i,j}(\partial_{j}X_{i})^{2}.

The two expressions agree when D​XDX is symmetric, but tr⁡((D​X)2)\operatorname{tr}((DX)^{2}) can have either sign for a general vector field. Thus (2.2) cannot be applied directly at an intermediate time: the potential of μt\mu_{t} need not have a useful Hessian lower bound, and the trace term has no sign for a general vector field with the prescribed divergence. Proposition 2.4 instead works at the endpoints, where the curvature bounds are available, and uses the symmetry of H​D​XHDX, with H=Hess⁡ΦH=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}, to recover the nonnegativity of the trace terms.

Definition 2.3 (Smooth Bochner couple).

Let T=∇ΦT=\nabla\Phi transport μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1} and set H=Hess⁡ΦH=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}. Given a smooth mean-zero datum gg and constants a0,a1≥0a_{0},a_{1}\geq 0, a pair of smooth vector fields (X,Y)(X,Y) is called a Bochner couple with datum gg and constants (a0,a1)(a_{0},a_{1}) if the relations

Y∘T=HX,−divμ0X=g,−(divμ1Y)∘T=g,Y\circ T=HX,\qquad-\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{0}}X=g,\qquad-(\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{1}}Y)\circ T=g, (2.6)

hold, the two matrix symmetry conditions

H​D​X​is symmetric,((D​Y)∘T)​H​is symmetricHDX\ \text{is symmetric},\qquad((DY)\circ T)H\ \text{is symmetric} (2.7)

hold, and the endpoint Bochner estimates

‖X‖L2​(μ0)≤a0​‖g‖L2​(μ0),‖Y‖L2​(μ1)≤a1​‖g‖L2​(μ0)\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}\leq a_{0}\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})},\qquad\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{1})}\leq a_{1}\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})} (2.8)

are valid. If there is a scalar function uu such that

X=H−1∇u,Y∘T=∇uX=H^{-1}\nabla u,\qquad Y\circ T=\nabla u (2.9)

then we say that the couple is generated by the weighted Poisson equation. Here H=D​T=Hess⁡ΦH=DT=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi} is the differential of the Brenier map that relates the two fields.

We call constructing a Bochner couple from common data and then interpolating its two fields Bochner coupling.

Proposition 2.4 (Endpoint estimates for the weighted Poisson equation).

For every g∈L2​(μ0)g\in L^{2}(\mu_{0}) with ∫g​d​μ0=0\int g\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}=0, there exists a unique u∈H1​(μ0)u\in H^{1}(\mu_{0}) satisfying ∫u​d​μ0=0\int u\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}=0 and

−divμ0(H−1∇u)=g-\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{0}}(H^{-1}\nabla u)=g (2.10)

in the weak sense. Setting X=H−1∇uX=H^{-1}\nabla u and defining YY by Y∘T=∇uY\circ T=\nabla u, one also has

−(divμ1Y)∘T=g-(\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{1}}Y)\circ T=g (2.11)

in the weak sense, together with the estimates

‖X‖L2​(μ0)≤κ0−1/2‖g‖L2​(μ0),‖Y‖L2​(μ1)=‖∇u‖L2​(μ0)≤κ1−1/2‖g‖L2​(μ0).\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}\leq\kappa_{0}^{-1/2}\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})},\qquad\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{1})}=\left\lVert\nabla u\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}\leq\kappa_{1}^{-1/2}\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}. (2.12)
Proof.

Step 1: Endpoint identities and Bochner estimates. We begin with u∈Cc∞​(ℝn)u\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). Set

X=H−1∇u,Bu=−divμ0X,Y(Tx)=∇u(x)=H(x)X(x).X=H^{-1}\nabla u,\qquad Bu=-\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{0}}X,\qquad Y(Tx)=\nabla u(x)=H(x)X(x).

Both fields are compactly supported, and we will verify that (X,Y)(X,Y) is a Bochner couple with datum B​uBu and constants (κ0−1/2,κ1−1/2)(\kappa_{0}^{-1/2},\kappa_{1}^{-1/2}). We first derive the endpoint estimates (the a priori estimates) with g=B​ug=Bu; the extension to an arbitrary mean-zero g∈L2​(μ0)g\in L^{2}(\mu_{0}) is carried out at the end of the proof by a density argument. For every ψ∈Cc∞​(ℝn)\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),

∫⟨∇ψ,Y⟩​d​μ1=∫⟨∇ψ​(T​x),H⁡(x)​X​(x)⟩​d​μ0​(x)=∫⟨∇(ψ∘T),X⟩​d​μ0,\int\left\langle\nabla\psi,Y\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{1}=\int\left\langle\nabla\psi(Tx),H(x)X(x)\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}(x)=\int\left\langle\nabla(\psi\circ T),X\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}, (2.13)

which implies

(divμ1⁡Y)∘T=divμ0⁡X=−B​u(\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{1}}Y)\circ T=\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{0}}X=-Bu (2.14)

in the weak sense. This transformation rule for weighted divergence under the Brenier map appears in [36, Lemma 2.1 and (2.5)]. Let P=D​XP=DX, so that Pk​j=∂jXkP_{kj}=\partial_{j}X_{k}. Since Hi​k=(Hess⁡Φ)i​k=∂i∂kΦH_{ik}=(\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi})_{ik}=\partial_{i}\partial_{k}\Phi, differentiating (H​X)i=∂iu(HX)_{i}=\partial_{i}u with respect to xjx_{j} yields

(Hess⁡u)i​j=(∂jHi​k)​Xk+Hi​k​Pk​j=Φi​k​j​Xk+Hi​k​Pk​j,(\operatorname{Hess}{u})_{ij}=(\partial_{j}H_{ik})X_{k}+H_{ik}P_{kj}=\Phi_{ikj}X_{k}+H_{ik}P_{kj}, (2.15)

and hence

Hess⁡u=CX+H​P,(CX)i​j=Φi​j​k​Xk.\operatorname{Hess}{u}=C_{X}+HP,\qquad(C_{X})_{ij}=\Phi_{ijk}X_{k}. (2.16)

The smoothness of Φ\Phi implies that CXC_{X} is symmetric. Since Hess⁡u\operatorname{Hess}{u} is symmetric as well, (2.16) shows that H​P=Hess⁡u−CXHP=\operatorname{Hess}{u}-C_{X} is symmetric. The matrix

H−1/2(HP)H−1/2=H1/2PH−1/2H^{-1/2}(HP)H^{-1/2}=H^{1/2}PH^{-1/2}

is symmetric and similar to PP. Hence,

tr(P2)=‖H−1/2(HP)H−1/2‖HS2≥0.\operatorname{tr}(P^{2})=\left\lVert H^{-1/2}(HP)H^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\geq 0. (2.17)

Applying Lemma 2.1 with μ0\mu_{0} and using (2.17), we obtain

‖X‖L2​(μ0)=‖H−1∇u‖L2​(μ0)≤κ0−1/2‖Bu‖L2​(μ0)=κ0−1/2‖g‖L2​(μ0).\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}=\left\lVert H^{-1}\nabla u\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}\leq\kappa_{0}^{-1/2}\left\lVert Bu\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}=\kappa_{0}^{-1/2}\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}. (2.18)

At the target, let Q⁡(x)=(Dy​Y)​(T​x)Q(x)=(D_{y}Y)(Tx). Since Y​(T​x)=∇u​(x)Y(Tx)=\nabla u(x), we have Q​H=Hess⁡uQH=\operatorname{Hess}{u}. Thus QQ is similar to the symmetric matrix H−1/2HessuH−1/2H^{-1/2}\operatorname{Hess}{u}H^{-1/2}, and hence

tr(Q2)=‖H−1/2HessuH−1/2‖HS2≥0.\operatorname{tr}(Q^{2})=\left\lVert H^{-1/2}\operatorname{Hess}{u}H^{-1/2}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\geq 0. (2.19)

Applying Lemma 2.1 with μ1\mu_{1}, together with (2.14) and (2.19), we obtain

‖Y‖L2​(μ1)=‖∇u‖L2​(μ0)≤κ1−1/2‖Bu‖L2​(μ0).\left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{1})}=\left\lVert\nabla u\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}\leq\kappa_{1}^{-1/2}\left\lVert Bu\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu_{0})}. (2.20)

Thus the two bounds are the endpoint estimates of a Bochner couple with constants (κ0−1/2,κ1−1/2)(\kappa_{0}^{-1/2},\kappa_{1}^{-1/2}).

Step 2: Weak solvability and range density. The existence and uniqueness of a centered weak solution of (2.10) already follow from the Lax–Milgram theorem [7, Corollary 5.8], applied on the mean-zero subspace of H1​(μ0)H^{1}(\mu_{0}) to the bilinear form

(v,w)⟼∫⟨H−1∇v,∇w⟩dμ0.(v,w)\longmapsto\int\left\langle H^{-1}\nabla v,\nabla w\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}.

≤12∫ηR2⟨H−1∇h,∇h⟩dμ0+2∫h2⟨H−1∇ηR,∇ηR⟩dμ0.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\int\eta_{R}^{2}\left\langle H^{-1}\nabla h,\nabla h\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}+2\int h^{2}\left\langle H^{-1}\nabla\eta_{R},\nabla\eta_{R}\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}.

Letting R→∞R\to\infty on each fixed ball yields ∇h=0\nabla h=0; the zero-mean condition then implies h=0h=0. Thus the range is dense.

Step 3: Approximation and passage to the limit. Choose uk0∈Cc∞​(ℝn)u_{k}^{0}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) such that B​uk0→gBu_{k}^{0}\to g in L2​(μ0)L^{2}(\mu_{0}), and set uk=uk0−∫uk0​d​μ0u_{k}=u_{k}^{0}-\int u_{k}^{0}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}. Then uku_{k} is centered, while ∇uk=∇uk0\nabla u_{k}=\nabla u_{k}^{0} and B​uk=B​uk0Bu_{k}=Bu_{k}^{0}. ∫⟨H−1∇u,∇φ⟩dμ0=limk→∞∫⟨H−1∇uk,∇φ⟩dμ0=limk→∞∫(Buk)φdμ0=∫gφdμ0.\displaystyle\int\left\langle H^{-1}\nabla u,\nabla\varphi\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\int\left\langle H^{-1}\nabla u_{k},\nabla\varphi\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\int(Bu_{k})\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}=\int g\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0}. Thus uu is a centered weak solution of (2.10). By the density of Cc∞​(ℝn)C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) in H1​(μ0)H^{1}(\mu_{0}), the weak identity extends to all H1​(μ0)H^{1}(\mu_{0}) test functions. Hence uu coincides with the unique solution provided by the Lax–Milgram theorem. Define YkY_{k} by Yk∘T=∇ukY_{k}\circ T=\nabla u_{k}. Since uk→uu_{k}\to u in H1​(μ0)H^{1}(\mu_{0}), we have Yk→YY_{k}\to Y in L2​(μ1)L^{2}(\mu_{1}). Applying (2.13) to uk0u_{k}^{0} and then passing to the limit, we obtain

∫⟨∇ψ,Y⟩​d​μ1=∫g​ψ∘T​d​μ0,ψ∈Cc∞​(ℝn),\int\left\langle\nabla\psi,Y\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{1}=\int g\,\psi\circ T\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{0},\qquad\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), (2.25)

which implies −(divμ1Y)∘T=g-(\operatorname{div}_{\mu_{1}}Y)\circ T=g in the weak sense. Passing to the limit in (2.18) and (2.20) yields (2.12). ∎

At the smooth level, the same Poisson solution uu gives both matrix identities. The matrix H​D​XHDX is symmetric at the source, and ((Dy​Y)∘T)​H=Hess⁡u((D_{y}Y)\circ T)H=\operatorname{Hess}{u} is symmetric at the target. These facts give the sharp endpoint estimates. They do not require a curvature bound for any intermediate measure. Together with (2.14), these estimates provide the input for the affine interpolation in Proposition 2.5.

Proposition 2.5 (Poincaré estimate in the smooth case).

Assume that Vi∈C∞​(ℝn)V_{i}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) and Hess⁡Vi⪰κi​I\operatorname{Hess}{V_{i}}\succeq\kappa_{i}I for i=0,1i=0,1. Apply Proposition 2.4 to g=h∘Ftg=h\circ F_{t} and denote X=H−1∇uX=H^{-1}\nabla u. Define qq at time tt by

3 Regularization and transport stability

To pass to nonsmooth endpoint potentials, we need a smooth approximation that preserves their curvature lower bounds. Gaussian convolution alone weakens these bounds, so we combine it with a compensating dilation. The covariance estimate needed to verify this regularization is the following linear form of the Brascamp–Lieb inequality.

Lemma 3.1.

Let U:ℝn→(−∞,+∞]U:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper and lower semicontinuous, with U−λ​|x|2/2U-\lambda|x|^{2}/2 convex for some λ>0\lambda>0. If 0<∫e−U​𝑑x<∞0<\int e^{-U}\,\mathrm{d}x<\infty, d​ν∝e−U​d​x\mathrm{d}\nu\propto e^{-U}\,\mathrm{d}x, and ζ\zeta has law ν\nu, then

Cov⁡(ζ)⪯λ−1​I.\operatorname{Cov}(\zeta)\preceq\lambda^{-1}I. (3.1)
Proof.

Write U=λ​|x|2/2+WU=\lambda|x|^{2}/2+W, where WW is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Choose an affine minorant W⁡(x)≥p⋅x+bW(x)\geq p\cdot x+b, and let

Wm​(x)=infy∈ℝn{W⁡(y)+m2​|x−y|2},m≥1,W_{m}(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\left\{W(y)+\frac{m}{2}|x-y|^{2}\right\},\qquad m\geq 1,

be the Moreau envelopes of WW. They are finite and convex, Wm↑WW_{m}\uparrow W pointwise, and

Wm​(x)≥p⋅x+b−|p|22​m.W_{m}(x)\geq p\cdot x+b-\frac{|p|^{2}}{2m}. (3.2)

Let ρ\rho be a smooth, compactly supported, radial probability density, write ρδ​(x)=δ−n​ρ​(x/δ)\rho_{\delta}(x)=\delta^{-n}\rho(x/\delta), and set Wm,δ=Wm∗ρδW_{m,\delta}=W_{m}*\rho_{\delta}. Then Wm,δW_{m,\delta} is smooth and convex. Because ∫z​ρδ​(z)​𝑑z=0\int z\rho_{\delta}(z)\,\mathrm{d}z=0, (3.2) also holds with Wm,δW_{m,\delta} in place of WmW_{m}.

The classical Brascamp–Lieb inequality [6], applied to the smooth potential λ​|x|2/2+Wm,δ\lambda|x|^{2}/2+W_{m,\delta}, gives

Varνm,δ⁡(a⋅x)≤λ−1​|a|2,a∈ℝn,\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{m,\delta}}(a\cdot x)\leq\lambda^{-1}|a|^{2},\qquad a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, (3.3)

where dνm,δ∝e−λ|x|2/2−Wm,δ(x)dx\mathrm{d}\nu_{m,\delta}\propto e^{-\lambda|x|^{2}/2-W_{m,\delta}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x. For fixed mm, the finite convex function WmW_{m} is continuous and Wm,δ→WmW_{m,\delta}\to W_{m} locally uniformly as δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0. Moreover, (3.2), uniformly for m≥1m\geq 1 and δ>0\delta>0, bounds all the corresponding unnormalized densities by a constant times e−λ|x|2/2−p⋅xe^{-\lambda|x|^{2}/2-p\cdot x}. This function remains integrable after multiplication by 1+|x|21+|x|^{2}, so dominated convergence applies to the normalization constants and to the first and second moments. We may first let δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0 in (3.3) and then let m→∞m\to\infty. Since Wm↑WW_{m}\uparrow W, this yields

Varν⁡(a⋅x)≤λ−1​|a|2,a∈ℝn,\operatorname{Var}_{\nu}(a\cdot x)\leq\lambda^{-1}|a|^{2},\qquad a\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

which is equivalent to the stated covariance bound. ∎

Lemma 3.2.

Let κ>0\kappa>0, and let μ\mu have potential VV with V−κ​|x|2/2V-\kappa|x|^{2}/2 convex. Let ξ∼μ\xi\sim\mu and G∼N⁡(0,I)G\sim N(0,I) be independent. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, define

ξε=ξ+ε​G1+κ​ε,με=Law⁡(ξε).\xi^{\varepsilon}=\frac{\xi+\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,G}{\sqrt{1+\kappa\varepsilon}},\qquad\mu^{\varepsilon}=\operatorname{Law}(\xi^{\varepsilon}).

Then με→μ\mu^{\varepsilon}\to\mu in W2W_{2}. The measure με\mu^{\varepsilon} has a smooth positive density e−Vεe^{-V^{\varepsilon}} whose potential satisfies

κ​I⪯Hess⁡Vε⪯1+κ​εε​I.\kappa I\preceq\operatorname{Hess}{V^{\varepsilon}}\preceq\frac{1+\kappa\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}I. (3.4)

The lower Hessian bound is also the classical convolution rule for strong log-concavity; see [46, Proposition 5.5]. We include the conditional-moment proof because it simultaneously gives the upper Hessian bound and covers extended-valued endpoint potentials.

Proof.

Step 1: Convergence in W2W_{2}. Set aε=1+κ​εa_{\varepsilon}=\sqrt{1+\kappa\varepsilon}. Writing V=κ​|x|2/2+WV=\kappa|x|^{2}/2+W with WW convex, choose an affine minorant W⁡(x)≥p⋅x+bW(x)\geq p\cdot x+b. Then e−V⁡(x)e^{-V(x)} is bounded by a constant times exp(−κ|x|2/2−p⋅x)\exp(-\kappa|x|^{2}/2-p\cdot x), and hence 𝔼​|ξ|2<∞\mathbb{E}|\xi|^{2}<\infty. Couple με\mu^{\varepsilon} and μ\mu by using the same pair (ξ,G)(\xi,G). By the definition of W2W_{2},

W22​(με,μ)\displaystyle W_{2}^{2}(\mu^{\varepsilon},\mu) ≤𝔼​|(aε−1−1)​ξ+εaε​G|2\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left|(a_{\varepsilon}^{-1}-1)\xi+\frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}{a_{\varepsilon}}G\right|^{2} (3.5)
=(aε−1−1)2​𝔼​|ξ|2+εaε2​𝔼​|G|2=(aε−1−1)2​𝔼​|ξ|2+ε​naε2⟶0,\displaystyle=(a_{\varepsilon}^{-1}-1)^{2}\mathbb{E}|\xi|^{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{a_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\mathbb{E}|G|^{2}=(a_{\varepsilon}^{-1}-1)^{2}\mathbb{E}|\xi|^{2}+\frac{\varepsilon n}{a_{\varepsilon}^{2}}\longrightarrow 0,

where the cross term vanishes since GG is independent of ξ\xi and 𝔼⁡[G]=0\mathbb{E}[G]=0. This proves με→μ\mu^{\varepsilon}\to\mu in W2W_{2}.

Step 2: Hessian bounds after Gaussian smoothing. Set Yε=ξ+ε​GY_{\varepsilon}=\xi+\sqrt{\varepsilon}G, let ϕε\phi_{\varepsilon} be the density of N⁡(0,ε​I)N(0,\varepsilon I), and write

pε​(y)=∫ϕε​(y−x)​𝑑μ​(x)=e−Uε​(y).p_{\varepsilon}(y)=\int\phi_{\varepsilon}(y-x)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)=e^{-U_{\varepsilon}(y)}. (3.6)

This density is smooth and strictly positive. For each y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, Bayes’ rule gives

ℙ⁡(ξ∈d​x∣Yε=y)=ϕε​(y−x)pε​(y)​d​μ​(x).\mathbb{P}(\xi\in\mathrm{d}x\mid Y_{\varepsilon}=y)=\frac{\phi_{\varepsilon}(y-x)}{p_{\varepsilon}(y)}\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x). (3.7)

Define mε​(y)=𝔼⁡[ξ∣Yε=y]m_{\varepsilon}(y)=\mathbb{E}[\xi\mid Y_{\varepsilon}=y]. Then, for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n,

pε​(y)​mε,j​(y)=∫xj​ϕε​(y−x)​𝑑μ​(x).p_{\varepsilon}(y)m_{\varepsilon,j}(y)=\int x_{j}\phi_{\varepsilon}(y-x)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x). (3.8)

For 1≤j,k≤n1\leq j,k\leq n, differentiation of (3.6) and (3.8) yields

∂kpε(y)=−ε−1∫(yk−xk)ϕε(y−x)dμ(x),\partial_{k}p_{\varepsilon}(y)=-\varepsilon^{-1}\int(y_{k}-x_{k})\phi_{\varepsilon}(y-x)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x), (3.9)

and

∂k(pε(y)mε,j(y))=−ε−1∫xj(yk−xk)ϕε(y−x)dμ(x).\partial_{k}\!\left(p_{\varepsilon}(y)m_{\varepsilon,j}(y)\right)=-\varepsilon^{-1}\int x_{j}(y_{k}-x_{k})\phi_{\varepsilon}(y-x)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x). (3.10)

The quotient rule therefore yields

∇log⁡pε​(y)=−ε−1​(y−mε​(y)),D​mε​(y)=ε−1​Cov⁡(ξ∣Yε=y).\nabla\log p_{\varepsilon}(y)=-\varepsilon^{-1}\bigl(y-m_{\varepsilon}(y)\bigr),\qquad Dm_{\varepsilon}(y)=\varepsilon^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\xi\mid Y_{\varepsilon}=y). (3.11)

Indeed, the (j,k)(j,k) entry in the second identity is ε−1​(𝔼⁡[ξj​ξk∣Yε=y]−mε,j​(y)​mε,k​(y))\varepsilon^{-1}\left(\mathbb{E}[\xi_{j}\xi_{k}\mid Y_{\varepsilon}=y]-m_{\varepsilon,j}(y)m_{\varepsilon,k}(y)\right). Since 𝔼​|ξ|2<∞\mathbb{E}|\xi|^{2}<\infty, differentiation under the integral sign is justified by dominated convergence, locally uniformly in yy. The first identity in (3.11) is the Gaussian Tweedie formula. The second expresses the derivative of the conditional mean in terms of the conditional covariance. See Efron [19] for the statistical formulation and Dytso, Poor, and Shamai [18] for vector Gaussian derivative identities. Since Uε=−log⁡pεU_{\varepsilon}=-\log p_{\varepsilon}, differentiating the first identity in (3.11) and substituting the formula for D​mεDm_{\varepsilon} yields

Hess⁡Uε​(y)=ε−1​I−ε−2​Cov⁡(ξ∣Yε=y).\operatorname{Hess}{U_{\varepsilon}}(y)=\varepsilon^{-1}I-\varepsilon^{-2}\operatorname{Cov}(\xi\mid Y_{\varepsilon}=y). (3.12)

Thus, up to an additive normalizing constant, the conditional law above has potential

x⟼V⁡(x)+|y−x|22​ε,x\longmapsto V(x)+\frac{|y-x|^{2}}{2\varepsilon},

which is (κ+ε−1)(\kappa+\varepsilon^{-1})-strongly convex in the extended-valued sense. Therefore, by Lemma 3.1,

Substituting (3.13) into (3.12) gives the lower Hessian bound, while Cov⁡(ξ∣Yε=y)⪰0\operatorname{Cov}(\xi\mid Y_{\varepsilon}=y)\succeq 0 gives the upper bound:

κ1+κ​ε​I⪯Hess⁡Uε⪯ε−1​I.\frac{\kappa}{1+\kappa\varepsilon}I\preceq\operatorname{Hess}{U_{\varepsilon}}\preceq\varepsilon^{-1}I. (3.14)

Finally, since ξε=Yε/aε\xi^{\varepsilon}=Y_{\varepsilon}/a_{\varepsilon} and aε2=1+κ​εa_{\varepsilon}^{2}=1+\kappa\varepsilon, the change of variables yields

Vε​(x)=Uε​(aε​x)−n​log⁡aε,Hess⁡Vε​(x)=aε2​Hess⁡Uε​(aε​x),V^{\varepsilon}(x)=U_{\varepsilon}(a_{\varepsilon}x)-n\log a_{\varepsilon},\qquad\operatorname{Hess}{V^{\varepsilon}}(x)=a_{\varepsilon}^{2}\operatorname{Hess}{U_{\varepsilon}}(a_{\varepsilon}x), (3.15)

which proves (3.4). ∎

Lemma 3.3 (Regularity and bounds for the Brenier map).

Let d​μi=e−Vi​d​x\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}=e^{-V_{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x, i=0,1i=0,1, be smooth positive probability densities whose potentials satisfy

λi−​I⪯Hess⁡Vi⪯λi+​I,0<λi−≤λi+<∞.\lambda_{i}^{-}I\preceq\operatorname{Hess}{V_{i}}\preceq\lambda_{i}^{+}I,\qquad 0<\lambda_{i}^{-}\leq\lambda_{i}^{+}<\infty.

Then the Brenier map T=∇ΦT=\nabla\Phi from μ0\mu_{0} to μ1\mu_{1} is a smooth global diffeomorphism and

λ0−λ1+​I⪯Hess⁡Φ⪯λ0+λ1−​I.\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{0}^{-}}{\lambda_{1}^{+}}}\,I\preceq\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}\preceq\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{0}^{+}}{\lambda_{1}^{-}}}\,I. (3.16)
Proof.

Since the endpoint densities are smooth and positive on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, they and their reciprocals are bounded on every compact set. Hence [12, Corollary 5], applied for every order of regularity, shows that T=∇ΦT=\nabla\Phi is a smooth global diffeomorphism. Moreover, its inverse is the reverse Brenier map S:μ1→μ0S:\mu_{1}\to\mu_{0}; see [12, Remark 4].

Caffarelli’s contraction theorem [9], in the two-potential form of [35, Theorem 2.2], applied first to TT and then to SS, yields

Lip⁡(T)≤λ0+λ1−,Lip⁡(S)≤λ1+λ0−.\operatorname{Lip}(T)\leq\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{0}^{+}}{\lambda_{1}^{-}}},\qquad\operatorname{Lip}(S)\leq\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{1}^{+}}{\lambda_{0}^{-}}}. (3.17)

Since S=T−1S=T^{-1} and both maps are smooth, we have D​S​(T⁡(x))=D​T​(x)−1DS(T(x))=DT(x)^{-1}. The preceding Lipschitz bounds therefore imply

λ0−λ1+​I⪯D​T=Hess⁡Φ⪯λ0+λ1−​I,\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{0}^{-}}{\lambda_{1}^{+}}}\,I\preceq DT=\operatorname{Hess}{\Phi}\preceq\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{0}^{+}}{\lambda_{1}^{-}}}\,I, (3.18)

which proves (3.16). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Apply Lemma 3.2 to both endpoints with their respective curvature constants. Let εj↓0\varepsilon_{j}\downarrow 0, denote the regularized endpoints by μij\mu_{i}^{j}, i=0,1i=0,1, and let πj\pi_{j} be their quadratic optimal plans. By Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3, the assumptions of Proposition 2.5 hold with the same lower curvature constants κi\kappa_{i}.

By the stability theorem for optimal transport plans [48, Theorem 5.20], every weak subsequential limit of (πj)(\pi_{j}) is optimal between μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1}. Brenier’s theorem [8] gives a unique quadratic optimal plan π\pi because μ0≪ℒn\mu_{0}\ll\mathcal{L}^{n}. Hence πj→π\pi_{j}\to\pi weakly. The marginals converge in W2W_{2}, so the joint second moments also converge. It follows from [48, Theorem 6.9] that πj→π\pi_{j}\to\pi in W2​(ℝn×ℝn)W_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}). Fix t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and let Lt​(x,y)=(1−t)​x+t​yL_{t}(x,y)=(1-t)x+ty. Since LtL_{t} is Lipschitz,

μtj:=(Lt)#​πj→(Lt)#​π=μtin ​W2.\mu_{t}^{j}:=(L_{t})_{\#}\pi_{j}\rightarrow(L_{t})_{\#}\pi=\mu_{t}\quad\text{in }W_{2}. (3.19)

For f∈Cc∞​(ℝn)f\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), by Proposition 2.5, we obtain

Varμtj⁡(f)≤(1−tκ0+tκ1)2​∫|∇f|2​d​μtj.\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_{t}^{j}}(f)\leq\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2}\int|\nabla f|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}^{j}. (3.20)

Since ff, f2f^{2}, and |∇f|2|\nabla f|^{2} are bounded and continuous, passing to the limit proves (1.1). Since t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] was arbitrary, the conclusion holds along the entire geodesic. ∎

4 Gaussian rigidity

Theorem 1.4 states that equality at an interior time is equivalent to a common Gaussian factor. The variances of the two Gaussian factors are κi−1\kappa_{i}^{-1}. We first prove a quantitative rigidity lemma at one endpoint. It shows that a near-extremizer of the Poincaré inequality has an almost constant gradient. We apply this lemma to regularized near-extremizers for μt\mu_{t}. The resulting limits are affine in the same direction at both endpoints, which gives the common Gaussian factorization. The converse follows by splitting the optimal transport along this Gaussian direction. Quantitative affine approximation of Poincaré near-extremizers for strongly log-concave measures was developed by De Philippis and Figalli [16, Section 4]. Courtade and Fathi proved an O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) squared L2L^{2}-gradient estimate for normalized near-extremizers [14, Lemma 2.2]. The next lemma is its rescaled, homogeneous one-function form; we include the short derivation to make the scaling explicit.

Lemma 4.1 (Homogeneous form of quantitative Poincaré stability).

Let ν\nu be the probability measure d​ν=e−W​d​x\mathrm{d}\nu=e^{-W}\,\mathrm{d}x, where WW is smooth and

Hess⁡W⪰κ​I,κ>0.\operatorname{Hess}{W}\succeq\kappa I,\qquad\kappa>0.

If h∈H1​(ν)h\in H^{1}(\nu) satisfies ∫h​𝑑ν=0\int h\,\mathrm{d}\nu=0, set

D=∫|∇h|2​𝑑ν−κ​∫h2​𝑑ν,a=∫∇h​𝑑ν.D=\int|\nabla h|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\nu-\kappa\int h^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\nu,\qquad a=\int\nabla h\,\mathrm{d}\nu.

Then D≥0D\geq 0 and

∫|∇h−a|2​𝑑ν≤9​D.\int|\nabla h-a|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\nu\leq 9D. (4.1)
Proof.

Since ∫h​𝑑ν=0\int h\,\mathrm{d}\nu=0, the Brascamp–Lieb inequality implies D≥0D\geq 0. The assertion is trivial when h=0h=0, so we may assume s:=‖h‖L2​(ν)>0s:=\left\lVert h\right\rVert_{L^{2}(\nu)}>0.

Define ν~=(x↦κ​x)#​ν\tilde{\nu}=(x\mapsto\sqrt{\kappa}x)_{\#}\nu and u⁡(z)=s−1​h​(z/κ)u(z)=s^{-1}h(z/\sqrt{\kappa}). Then ν~\tilde{\nu} is 11-strongly log-concave and

∫u​𝑑ν~=0,∫u2​𝑑ν~=1,∫|∇u|2​𝑑ν~=1+Dκ​s2.\int u\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}=0,\qquad\int u^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}=1,\qquad\int|\nabla u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}=1+\frac{D}{\kappa s^{2}}. (4.2)

Applying [14, Lemma 2.2] with k=1k=1, we obtain a unit vector w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n} such that

∫|∇u−w|2​𝑑ν~≤9​Dκ​s2.\int|\nabla u-w|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}\leq\frac{9D}{\kappa s^{2}}. (4.3)

Since a=∫∇h​𝑑νa=\int\nabla h\,\mathrm{d}\nu minimizes c⟼∫|∇h−c|2​𝑑νc\longmapsto\int|\nabla h-c|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\nu over c∈ℝnc\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

∫|∇h−a|2​𝑑ν≤∫|∇h−κ​s​w|2​𝑑ν=κ​s2​∫|∇u−w|2​𝑑ν~≤9​D.\int|\nabla h-a|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\nu\leq\int|\nabla h-\sqrt{\kappa}s\,w|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\nu=\kappa s^{2}\int|\nabla u-w|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\nu}\leq 9D. (4.4)

∎

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Step 1: Alignment of the vector fields. Fix t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) and first suppose

CP​(μt)=(1−tκ0+tκ1)2.C_{P}(\mu_{t})=\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2}. (4.5)

Choose φj∈Cc∞​(ℝn)\varphi_{j}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) such that

Varμt⁡(φj)=1,∫|∇φj|2​d​μt→(1−tκ0+tκ1)−2.\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_{t}}(\varphi_{j})=1,\qquad\int|\nabla\varphi_{j}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}\rightarrow\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{-2}. (4.6)

For ε>0\varepsilon>0, let μiε\mu_{i}^{\varepsilon} be the regularization of μi\mu_{i} given by Lemma 3.2, and let μtε\mu_{t}^{\varepsilon} be the corresponding interpolated measure. Set Xt=(1−t)​X0+t​X1X_{t}=(1-t)X_{0}+tX_{1}, so that Xt∼μtX_{t}\sim\mu_{t} and mt=(1−t)​m0+t​m1m_{t}=(1-t)m_{0}+tm_{1}. Hence

ℓt​(Xt)=(1−t)​S0+t​S1=((1−t)+t​κ0κ1)​S0.\ell_{t}(X_{t})=(1-t)S_{0}+tS_{1}=\left((1-t)+t\sqrt{\frac{\kappa_{0}}{\kappa_{1}}}\right)S_{0}. (4.35)

Consequently, since Var⁡(S0)=κ0−1\operatorname{Var}(S_{0})=\kappa_{0}^{-1} and ∇ℓt=e\nabla\ell_{t}=e with |e|=1|e|=1, we obtain

Varμt⁡(ℓt)=(1−tκ0+tκ1)2,∫|∇ℓt|2​d​μt=1.\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_{t}}(\ell_{t})=\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2},\qquad\int|\nabla\ell_{t}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}=1. (4.36)

Although ℓt\ell_{t} is not compactly supported, its standard cutoffs ℓt,R​(x)=χ⁡(x/R)​ℓt​(x)\ell_{t,R}(x)=\chi(x/R)\ell_{t}(x), where χ∈Cc∞​(ℝn)\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) is radial, χ=1\chi=1 on B1B_{1}, and supp⁡χ⊆B2\operatorname{supp}\chi\subseteq B_{2}, satisfy

ℓt,R⟶ℓtin ​H1​(μt).\ell_{t,R}\longrightarrow\ell_{t}\qquad\text{in }H^{1}(\mu_{t}). (4.37)

Indeed,

∇ℓt,R=χ⁡(x/R)​e+R−1​ℓt​(x)​(∇χ)​(x/R),\nabla\ell_{t,R}=\chi(x/R)e+R^{-1}\ell_{t}(x)(\nabla\chi)(x/R), (4.38)

and the convergence follows from μt∈𝒫2​(ℝn)\mu_{t}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}).

Therefore, by the definition of the Poincaré constant and the convergences in (4.37),

CP​(μt)≥limR→∞Varμt⁡(ℓt,R)∫|∇ℓt,R|2​d​μt=(1−tκ0+tκ1)2.C_{P}(\mu_{t})\geq\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\mu_{t}}(\ell_{t,R})}{\int|\nabla\ell_{t,R}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{t}}=\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2}. (4.39)

Combining with Theorem 1.1 proves the result. Replacing tt by any s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1] in (4.37) and (4.39) proves equality at every time. ∎

The equality argument identifies all common Gaussian directions, not only a single one. This yields the following maximal factorization.

Proposition 4.2 (Maximal common Gaussian factor).

Let μi\mu_{i} be κi\kappa_{i}-strongly log-concave probability measures on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, let mi=∫x​d​μim_{i}=\int x\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}, and define

E={v∈ℝn:∫v⋅∇ψdμi=κi∫v⋅(x−mi)ψdμi,∀ψ∈Cc∞(ℝn),i=0,1}.E=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\int v\cdot\nabla\psi\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}=\kappa_{i}\int v\cdot(x-m_{i})\psi\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{i},\quad\forall\,\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\quad i=0,1\right\}. (4.40)

Then EE is a linear subspace. Moreover, under the orthogonal identification ℝn=E⊕E⟂\mathbb{R}^{n}=E\oplus E^{\perp}, there exist νi∈𝒫⁡(E⟂)\nu_{i}\in\mathcal{P}(E^{\perp}) such that

μi=NE(PEmi,κi−1IE)⊗νi,i=0,1.\mu_{i}=N_{E}(P_{E}m_{i},\kappa_{i}^{-1}I_{E})\otimes\nu_{i},\qquad i=0,1. (4.41)

Here NEN_{E} denotes a Gaussian law on EE. If a subspace F⊆ℝnF\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} admits such a factorization for both endpoints, with respective covariances κi−1​IF\kappa_{i}^{-1}I_{F}, then F⊆EF\subseteq E. Thus EE is the unique maximal common Gaussian subspace. Moreover, equality in Theorem 1.1 at one (equivalently, every) time t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) holds if and only if E≠{0}E\neq\{0\}.

Proof.

The defining identities in (4.40) are linear in vv, so EE is a linear subspace. Fix i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\} and set s=PE​(x−mi)s=P_{E}(x-m_{i}) and z=PE⟂​(x−mi)z=P_{E^{\perp}}(x-m_{i}). For τ∈E\tau\in E and ξ∈E⟂\xi\in E^{\perp}, let ϕi​(τ,ξ)=∫ei⁡(τ⋅s+ξ⋅z)​d​μi\phi_{i}(\tau,\xi)=\int e^{\,\mathrm{i}(\tau\cdot s+\xi\cdot z)}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}. Applying (4.40) to cut-off approximations of the exponential, exactly as in the proof of Theorem 1.4, we obtain

v⋅∇τϕi​(τ,ξ)=−κi−1​(v⋅τ)​ϕi​(τ,ξ),for every v∈E,v\cdot\nabla_{\tau}\phi_{i}(\tau,\xi)=-\kappa_{i}^{-1}(v\cdot\tau)\phi_{i}(\tau,\xi),\qquad\text{for every $v\in E$}, (4.42)

which implies ∇τϕi​(τ,ξ)=−κi−1​τ​ϕi​(τ,ξ)\nabla_{\tau}\phi_{i}(\tau,\xi)=-\kappa_{i}^{-1}\tau\phi_{i}(\tau,\xi), and hence ϕi(τ,ξ)=e−|τ|2/(2κi)ϕi(0,ξ)\phi_{i}(\tau,\xi)=e^{-|\tau|^{2}/(2\kappa_{i})}\phi_{i}(0,\xi). By uniqueness of characteristic functions, this factorization shows that s∼NE​(0,κi−1​IE)s\sim N_{E}(0,\kappa_{i}^{-1}I_{E}) and is independent of zz; after recentering, this yields (4.41).

Conversely, if both endpoints split off Gaussian factors on a subspace FF with covariances κi−1​IF\kappa_{i}^{-1}I_{F}, then Gaussian integration by parts shows that every v∈Fv\in F satisfies (4.40). Hence F⊆EF\subseteq E, so EE is the unique maximal common Gaussian subspace. Finally, Theorem 1.4 shows that equality at an interior time is equivalent to E≠{0}E\neq\{0\}. ∎

Proposition 4.2 gives the following geometric description in the extended-valued case. For a closed convex set KK, let Lin⁡(K):={v:K+ℝ​v=K}\operatorname{Lin}(K):=\{v:K+\mathbb{R}v=K\} denote its lineality space.

Corollary 4.3 (Conditioned Gaussian measures).

Let Ki⊆ℝnK_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be convex Borel sets with nonempty interior, let κi>0\kappa_{i}>0, and let μi\mu_{i} be the probability measures with densities

dμi(x)∝e−κi|x|2/2𝟏Ki(x)dx,i=0,1.\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}(x)\propto e^{-\kappa_{i}|x|^{2}/2}\mathbf{1}_{K_{i}}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad i=0,1.

Then their quadratic Wasserstein interpolation satisfies

CP​(μt)≤(1−tκ0+tκ1)2,0≤t≤1.C_{P}(\mu_{t})\leq\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2},\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1. (4.43)

Equality holds for some t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) if and only if

Lin⁡(K¯0)∩Lin⁡(K¯1)≠{0}.\operatorname{Lin}(\bar{K}_{0})\cap\operatorname{Lin}(\bar{K}_{1})\neq\{0\}. (4.44)

In that case equality holds for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. In particular, if either K0K_{0} or K1K_{1} is bounded, then

CP​(μt)<(1−tκ0+tκ1)2,for every ​t∈(0,1).C_{P}(\mu_{t})<\left(\frac{1-t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{0}}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{\kappa_{1}}}\right)^{2},\qquad\text{for every }t\in(0,1). (4.45)
Proof.

Since the boundary of a convex set with nonempty interior has Lebesgue measure zero, replacing KiK_{i} by K¯i\bar{K}_{i} does not change μi\mu_{i}. We may assume that both sets are closed. Up to additive constants, the extended-valued endpoint potentials are Vi​(x)=κi2​|x|2+ιKi​(x)V_{i}(x)=\frac{\kappa_{i}}{2}|x|^{2}+\iota_{K_{i}}(x), where ιKi\iota_{K_{i}} is zero on KiK_{i} and +∞+\infty on KicK_{i}^{c}. Hence Theorem 1.1 implies the asserted inequality.

Suppose first that the two lineality spaces contain a common unit vector ee. Denote Ki′=Ki∩e⟂K_{i}^{\prime}=K_{i}\cap e^{\perp}. We claim that Ki=ℝ​e+Ki′K_{i}=\mathbb{R}e+K_{i}^{\prime}. Indeed, Ki+ℝ​e=KiK_{i}+\mathbb{R}e=K_{i}, and subtracting the ee-component of any point of KiK_{i} leaves a point of Ki′K_{i}^{\prime}. The Gaussian density therefore factorizes under ℝn=ℝ​e⊕e⟂\mathbb{R}^{n}=\mathbb{R}e\oplus e^{\perp}, and hence μi=N⁡(0,κi−1)⊗νi\mu_{i}=N(0,\kappa_{i}^{-1})\otimes\nu_{i}, where νi\nu_{i} is the corresponding conditioned Gaussian measure on Ki′K_{i}^{\prime}. The converse part of Theorem 1.4 yields equality at every time.

Conversely, by Theorem 1.4, equality at an interior time gives a common Gaussian line factor. Since the density of μi\mu_{i} is positive on int⁡Ki\operatorname{int}K_{i} and Ki=cl⁡(int⁡Ki)K_{i}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}K_{i}), its support is KiK_{i}. On the other hand, the support of the product in (1.2) has the form ℝ​e+supp⁡νi\mathbb{R}e+\operatorname{supp}\nu_{i}. It is invariant under translation by ℝ​e\mathbb{R}e, and therefore e∈Lin⁡(Ki)e\in\operatorname{Lin}(K_{i}) for both endpoints. Finally, a bounded convex set has trivial lineality space, which proves the strict inequality in the last assertion. ∎

5 Gaussian entropy and functional inequalities

We now apply the Poincaré interpolation theorem to the second variation of Gaussian relative entropy. Throughout this section, γ\gamma denotes the standard Gaussian measure, and 𝒫2​(ℝn)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) denotes the probability measures on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with finite second moment. We write

L=Δ−x⋅∇,Γ2(u)=‖Hessu‖HS2+|∇u|2L=\Delta-x\cdot\nabla,\qquad\Gamma_{2}(u)=\left\lVert\operatorname{Hess}{u}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}+|\nabla u|^{2}

for the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator and its iterated carré du champ, respectively. We also write Ps=es​LP_{s}=e^{sL} for the associated Markov semigroup on functions and Ps∗P_{s}^{*} for its dual action on probability measures.

All the entropies appearing below are finite. Indeed, relative to γ\gamma, a 11-strongly log-concave endpoint has density e−We^{-W} with WW convex, possibly extended-valued. Since WW is bounded below by an affine function, its negative part grows at most linearly, while s​e−s≤e−1se^{-s}\leq e^{-1} for s≥0s\geq 0 controls its positive part. Thus Entγ⁡(μi)<∞\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu_{i})<\infty. Moreover,

Entγ⁡(μ)=Entℒn⁡(μ)+12​∫|x|2​𝑑μ+n2​log⁡(2​π).\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu)=\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathcal{L}^{n}}(\mu)+\frac{1}{2}\int|x|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu+\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi).

The second moment remains finite along the Wasserstein geodesic, and Entℒn\operatorname{Ent}_{\mathcal{L}^{n}} is displacement convex [41]. Hence Entγ⁡(μt)<∞\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu_{t})<\infty for every t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1].

When the mean is zero, the estimate below follows the argument in [3, Theorem 4.6], which subtracts a quadratic polynomial. In Lemma 5.1, we separate the translation component. This removes the zero-average and symmetry assumptions. The local-to-global comparison and the subsequent functional estimates follow the arguments used by Aishwarya and Rotem [3, Sections 4–5] and by Aishwarya and Li [2, proof of Theorem 1.7] to derive functional inequalities from entropy. We prove the changes required by the translation component and cite each unchanged step at the point where it is used.

Lemma 5.1 (Γ2\Gamma_{2} estimate with the mean separated).

Let μ∈𝒫2​(ℝn)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) satisfy CP​(μ)≤1C_{P}(\mu)\leq 1, and let u∈C∞​(ℝn)u\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) satisfy ∇u,Hess⁡u∈L2​(μ)\nabla u,\operatorname{Hess}{u}\in L^{2}(\mu). Denote

m=∫x​𝑑μ,a=∫∇u​𝑑μ,ℓ=∫L​u​𝑑μ.m=\int x\,\mathrm{d}\mu,\qquad a=\int\nabla u\,\mathrm{d}\mu,\qquad\ell=\int Lu\,\mathrm{d}\mu.

Then

∫Γ2​(u)​𝑑μ≥2​∫|∇u|2​𝑑μ−|a|2+(ℓ+m⋅a)2n+(ℓ+m⋅a)2n2​∫|x−m|2​𝑑μ.\int\Gamma_{2}(u)\,\mathrm{d}\mu\geq 2\int|\nabla u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu-|a|^{2}+\frac{(\ell+m\cdot a)^{2}}{n}+\frac{(\ell+m\cdot a)^{2}}{n^{2}}\int|x-m|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu. (5.1)
Proof.

The proof follows [3, Theorem 4.6]; we give the modifications involving mm and aa. First suppose that a=0a=0. Set λ=ℓ/n\lambda=\ell/n and define v⁡(x)=u⁡(x)−λ2​|x−m|2v(x)=u(x)-\frac{\lambda}{2}|x-m|^{2}. Then ∫∇v​𝑑μ=0\int\nabla v\,\mathrm{d}\mu=0. The derivative ∂jv\partial_{j}v need not be compactly supported. We therefore apply the Poincaré inequality to ηR​∂jv\eta_{R}\partial_{j}v, where ηR\eta_{R} is a standard radial cut-off, and then let R→∞R\to\infty. This is the same cut-off argument used in the proof of Theorem 1.4. The error terms vanish since ∇v,Hess⁡v∈L2​(μ)\nabla v,\operatorname{Hess}{v}\in L^{2}(\mu). Summing over j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, gives

Expanding (5.2) and using ∇v=∇u−λ⁡(x−m)\nabla v=\nabla u-\lambda(x-m) and Hess⁡v=Hess⁡u−λ​I\operatorname{Hess}{v}=\operatorname{Hess}{u}-\lambda I, we obtain

∫‖Hess⁡u‖HS2​dμ−2​λ​∫Δ​u​dμ+n​λ2\displaystyle\int\left\lVert\operatorname{Hess}{u}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu-2\lambda\int\Delta u\,\mathrm{d}\mu+n\lambda^{2} ≥∫|∇u|2​𝑑μ\displaystyle\geq\int|\nabla u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu (5.3)
−2λ∫(x−m)⋅∇udμ+λ2∫|x−m|2dμ.\displaystyle-2\lambda\int(x-m)\cdot\nabla u\,\mathrm{d}\mu+\lambda^{2}\int|x-m|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu.

Since a=0a=0, ∫(Δ​u−(x−m)⋅∇u)​𝑑μ=ℓ\int\bigl(\Delta u-(x-m)\cdot\nabla u\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\ell. Thus,

∫‖Hess⁡u‖HS2​𝑑μ\displaystyle\int\left\lVert\operatorname{Hess}{u}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu ≥∫|∇u|2​𝑑μ+2​λ​ℓ−n​λ2+λ2​∫|x−m|2​𝑑μ\displaystyle\geq\int|\nabla u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu+2\lambda\ell-n\lambda^{2}+\lambda^{2}\int|x-m|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu (5.4)
=∫|∇u|2​dμ+ℓ2n+ℓ2n2​∫|x−m|2​dμ,\displaystyle=\int|\nabla u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu+\frac{\ell^{2}}{n}+\frac{\ell^{2}}{n^{2}}\int|x-m|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu,

which implies (5.1) when a=0a=0.

For general aa, apply the case a=0a=0 to w⁡(x)=u⁡(x)−a⋅xw(x)=u(x)-a\cdot x. Then

∫∇w​𝑑μ=0,∫L​w​𝑑μ=ℓ+m⋅a,∫|∇w|2​𝑑μ=∫|∇u|2​𝑑μ−|a|2.\int\nabla w\,\mathrm{d}\mu=0,\qquad\int Lw\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\ell+m\cdot a,\qquad\int|\nabla w|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\int|\nabla u|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu-|a|^{2}. (5.5)

Since Hess⁡w=Hess⁡u\operatorname{Hess}{w}=\operatorname{Hess}{u},

∫Γ2​(w)​𝑑μ=∫Γ2​(u)​𝑑μ−|a|2.\int\Gamma_{2}(w)\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\int\Gamma_{2}(u)\,\mathrm{d}\mu-|a|^{2}. (5.6)

Applying the estimate for the case a=0a=0 to ww then yields (5.1). ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

Step 1: Entropy variations. First assume that the endpoint potentials are smooth with two-sided Hessian bounds. Let ∇θt\nabla\theta_{t} be the velocity of the constant-speed geodesic, so

∂tμt+div(μt∇θt)=0,∂tθt+12|∇θt|2=0.\partial_{t}\mu_{t}+\operatorname{div}(\mu_{t}\nabla\theta_{t})=0,\qquad\partial_{t}\theta_{t}+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\theta_{t}|^{2}=0. (5.7)

where the assumed regularity and Gaussian tails justify the differentiations and integrations by parts above via standard radial cutoffs.

Theorem 5.2 (Gaussian BBL inequality with barycenter terms).

Fix t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) and p∈[0,∞]p\in[0,\infty]. Let f,g,h≥0f,g,h\geq 0 be γ\gamma-integrable, with ff and gg log-concave, and set A=∫f​𝑑γ>0A=\int f\,\mathrm{d}\gamma>0 and B=∫g​𝑑γ>0B=\int g\,\mathrm{d}\gamma>0. Assume that

Denote bt=(1−t)​bf+t​bgb_{t}=(1-t)b_{f}+tb_{g} and r=p/(1+n​p)r=p/(1+np), with r=1/nr=1/n when p=∞p=\infty. Then

∫hdγ≥e−|bt|2/2Mrt(Ae|bf|2/2,Be|bg|2/2).\int h\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\geq e^{-|b_{t}|^{2}/2}M_{r}^{t}\!\left(Ae^{|b_{f}|^{2}/2},Be^{|b_{g}|^{2}/2}\right). (5.25)

∫h​𝑑γ≥Mrt​(A,B).\int h\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\geq M_{r}^{t}(A,B). (5.26)
Proof.

We modify the argument of [2, Theorem 1.7] in two places to account for nonzero barycenters. Set F=log⁡fF=\log f, G=log⁡gG=\log g and H=log⁡hH=\log h on their respective positivity sets. If (X,Y)(X,Y) is an optimal coupling of μf\mu_{f} and μg\mu_{g}, and μt\mu_{t} is the law of (1−t)​X+t​Y(1-t)X+tY, then Jensen’s inequality and Donsker–Varadhan duality yield

∫h​𝑑γ≥Mpt​(e∫F​d​μf,e∫G​d​μg)​e−Entγ⁡(μt).\int h\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\geq M_{p}^{t}\!\left(e^{\int F\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{f}},e^{\int G\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{g}}\right)e^{-\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu_{t})}. (5.27)

Truncating the logarithms in the Donsker–Varadhan variational formula [17, Section 2] covers vanishing or unbounded functions, and the cases p=0,∞p=0,\infty follow by passage to the limit.

The measures μf\mu_{f} and μg\mu_{g} are 11-strongly log-concave, and the sine coefficients in (1.3) dominate their affine counterparts. Therefore, Theorem 1.5 gives

e−𝒟⁡(μt)≥M1/nt​(e−𝒟⁡(μf),e−𝒟⁡(μg)).e^{-\mathcal{D}(\mu_{t})}\geq M_{1/n}^{t}\!\left(e^{-\mathcal{D}(\mu_{f})},e^{-\mathcal{D}(\mu_{g})}\right). (5.29)

We use the following two-point form of the weighted Hölder inequality:

which is the weighted Hölder inequality with 1/r=1/p+n1/r=1/p+n; the cases p=0p=0 and p=∞p=\infty follow by continuity. Since the barycenter of μt\mu_{t} is btb_{t}, combining (5.27), (5.29), and (5.30) gives

e∫F​d​μf−𝒟⁡(μf)=A​e|bf|2/2,e∫G​d​μg−𝒟⁡(μg)=B​e|bg|2/2,e^{\int F\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{f}-\mathcal{D}(\mu_{f})}=Ae^{|b_{f}|^{2}/2},\qquad e^{\int G\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{g}-\mathcal{D}(\mu_{g})}=Be^{|b_{g}|^{2}/2}, (5.32)

We conclude with the functional inequalities obtained by joining a measure to equilibrium. This is the HWI principle of Otto and Villani [44], now applied with the centered entropy estimate. The even versions of the resulting HWI, logarithmic Sobolev, and Talagrand inequalities appear in [3, Section 5]; the centering argument in the proof of Corollary 5.5 removes the evenness assumption. If d​μ=ρ​d​γ\mathrm{d}\mu=\rho\,\mathrm{d}\gamma, denote

Iγ​(μ)=∫|∇log⁡ρ|2​𝑑μ\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\mu)=\int|\nabla\log\rho|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mu

for relative Fisher information, with the usual value +∞+\infty outside its form domain.

Corollary 5.5 (Gaussian functional inequalities after centering).

Let μ\mu be 11-strongly log-concave, let m=∫x​𝑑μm=\int x\,\mathrm{d}\mu, and denote

𝒟=Entγ⁡(μ)−12​|m|2,ℐ=Iγ​(μ)−|m|2,𝒲2=W22​(μ,γ)−|m|2.\mathcal{D}=\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu)-\frac{1}{2}|m|^{2},\quad\mathcal{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\mu)-|m|^{2},\quad\mathcal{W}^{2}=W_{2}^{2}(\mu,\gamma)-|m|^{2}.

Then 𝒟≥0\mathcal{D}\geq 0, ℐ≥0\mathcal{I}\geq 0, and 0≤𝒲2≤n0\leq\mathcal{W}^{2}\leq n. Moreover,

e𝒟/n≤cos⁡(2n​𝒲)+sin⁡(2/n​𝒲)2​n​ℐ,e^{\mathcal{D}/n}\leq\cos\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}\,\mathcal{W}\right)+\frac{\sin\!\left(\sqrt{2/n}\,\mathcal{W}\right)}{\sqrt{2n}}\sqrt{\mathcal{I}}, (5.38)
4​𝒟≤2​n​(e2​𝒟/n−1)≤ℐ,4\mathcal{D}\leq 2n\left(e^{2\mathcal{D}/n}-1\right)\leq\mathcal{I}, (5.39)

and

𝒲2≤−n​log⁡cos⁡(2n​𝒲)≤𝒟.\mathcal{W}^{2}\leq-n\log\cos\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}\,\mathcal{W}\right)\leq\mathcal{D}. (5.40)

Moreover, for every s≥0s\geq 0,

Entγ⁡(Ps∗​μ)≤e−4​s​(Entγ⁡(μ)−12​|m|2)+12​e−2​s​|m|2.\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(P_{s}^{*}\mu)\leq e^{-4s}\left(\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu)-\frac{1}{2}|m|^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2}e^{-2s}|m|^{2}. (5.41)
Proof.

Step 1: Centering. Let μ¯=(x↦x−m)#​μ\bar{\mu}=(x\mapsto x-m)_{\#}\mu be the centered translate of μ\mu. Set d​μ=ρ​d​γ\mathrm{d}\mu=\rho\,\mathrm{d}\gamma and ρ¯=d​μ¯/d​γ\bar{\rho}=\mathrm{d}\bar{\mu}/\mathrm{d}\gamma. Gaussian integration by parts and a change of variables give

∫∇log⁡ρ​𝑑μ=∫∇ρ​𝑑γ=m,log⁡ρ¯​(x)=log⁡ρ⁡(x+m)−m⋅x−|m|22,\int\nabla\log\rho\,\mathrm{d}\mu=\int\nabla\rho\,\mathrm{d}\gamma=m,\qquad\log\bar{\rho}(x)=\log\rho(x+m)-m\cdot x-\frac{|m|^{2}}{2}, (5.42)

where the Gaussian integration by parts in the first identity is justified by standard radial cutoffs whenever Iγ​(μ)<∞\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\mu)<\infty. If Iγ​(μ)=+∞\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\mu)=+\infty, the identity for the translated density implies Iγ​(μ¯)=+∞\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\bar{\mu})=+\infty, so the Fisher-information identity below holds in the extended sense. Combining this with the orthogonal decomposition of the quadratic transport cost, we obtain

𝒟=Entγ⁡(μ¯),ℐ=Iγ​(μ¯),𝒲=W2​(μ¯,γ),\mathcal{D}=\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\bar{\mu}),\qquad\mathcal{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\bar{\mu}),\qquad\mathcal{W}=W_{2}(\bar{\mu},\gamma), (5.43)

which yields the asserted nonnegativity. Hence it is sufficient to assume m=0m=0.

Set ω=2/n​𝒲\omega=\sqrt{2/n}\,\mathcal{W}. In the smooth case, let TT be the Brenier map from γ\gamma to μ¯\bar{\mu}. Since both measures are centered, ∫(T⁡(x)−x)​𝑑γ​(x)=0\int(T(x)-x)\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x)=0, while Caffarelli’s contraction theorem [9] yields 0⪯D​T⪯I0\preceq DT\preceq I. Applying the Gaussian Poincaré inequality to each component of T−IT-I and summing over the components, we obtain

𝒲2=∫|T⁡(x)−x|2​𝑑γ​(x)≤∫‖D​T−I‖HS2​𝑑γ≤n.\mathcal{W}^{2}=\int|T(x)-x|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma(x)\leq\int\left\lVert DT-I\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\gamma\leq n. (5.44)

The general case follows by Lemma 3.2. In particular, 0≤ω≤2<π/20\leq\omega\leq\sqrt{2}<\pi/2.

Step 2: HWI, logarithmic Sobolev, and Talagrand estimates. First assume that μ¯\bar{\mu} has a smooth potential with two-sided Hessian bounds. Apply Theorem 1.5 to the geodesic from μ¯\bar{\mu} to γ\gamma, and write Et=Entγ⁡(μt)E_{t}=\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu_{t}). Differentiating the finite-time inequality at the first endpoint and using −E0′≤Iγ​(μ¯)​W2​(μ¯,γ)-E_{0}^{\prime}\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\bar{\mu})}\,W_{2}(\bar{\mu},\gamma) yields (5.38), as in [3, Theorem 5.5]. Squaring this inequality and arguing as in [3, Corollary 5.6] yields (5.39). Reversing the geodesic and differentiating at the Gaussian endpoint, where the Fisher information vanishes, yields e−𝒟/n≤cosωe^{-\mathcal{D}/n}\leq\cos\omega. Together with −log⁡cos⁡ω≥ω2/2-\log\cos\omega\geq\omega^{2}/2, this yields (5.40), as in [3, Corollary 5.11]. Once Theorem 1.5 has replaced the even entropy estimate used there, none of these arguments requires symmetry.

Since Ps∗​μ¯P_{s}^{*}\bar{\mu} remains centered and 11-strongly log-concave, the de Bruijn argument as in [3, Corollary 5.9] applied with (5.39) yields

Entγ⁡(Ps∗​μ¯)≤e−4​s​Entγ⁡(μ¯).\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(P_{s}^{*}\bar{\mu})\leq e^{-4s}\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\bar{\mu}). (5.45)

The mean of Ps∗​μP_{s}^{*}\mu is e−s​me^{-s}m, and its centered translate is Ps∗​μ¯P_{s}^{*}\bar{\mu}. The Gaussian entropy translation formula therefore yields (5.41).

For the general case, set με=Pε∗​μ¯\mu_{\varepsilon}=P_{\varepsilon}^{*}\bar{\mu}. By Lemma 3.2, applied with parameter e2​ε−1e^{2\varepsilon}-1, these measures satisfy the required smooth two-sided Hessian bounds and converge to μ¯\bar{\mu} in W2W_{2}. Moreover, the data processing inequality, lower semicontinuity, and the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck gradient commutation give

Entγ⁡(με)⟶Entγ⁡(μ¯),Iγ​(με)≤e−2​ε​Iγ​(μ¯).\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu_{\varepsilon})\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\bar{\mu}),\qquad\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\mu_{\varepsilon})\leq e^{-2\varepsilon}\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\bar{\mu}). (5.46)

These facts allow passage to the limit in (5.38), (5.39) and (5.40). For (5.41), use Ps∗​με=Ps+ε∗​μ¯P_{s}^{*}\mu_{\varepsilon}=P_{s+\varepsilon}^{*}\bar{\mu} and the lower semicontinuity of entropy before letting ε→0\varepsilon\to 0. ∎

Remark 5.6.

The two rates in (5.41) are optimal. Translates of γ\gamma attain the e−2​se^{-2s} term, while centered Gaussian contractions with covariance approaching II show that e−4​se^{-4s} cannot be improved for centered measures. For a centered 11-strongly log-concave measure, the result of Bobkov, Gozlan, Roberto, and Samson [5, Corollary 2.2] gives

n⁡(e2​Entγ​(μ)/n−1)≤Iγ​(μ).n\left(e^{2\operatorname{Ent}_{\gamma}(\mu)/n}-1\right)\leq\mathrm{I}_{\gamma}(\mu).

Under the same centering and curvature assumptions, (5.39) doubles the left-hand side. This improvement uses the full geodesic Poincaré estimate.

Appendix A Failure of interpolation by the endpoint Poincaré constants

Proposition A.1.

There exist κ>0\kappa>0 and two κ\kappa-strongly log-concave probability measures μ0,μ1\mu_{0},\mu_{1} on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, such that their Wasserstein midpoint satisfies

CP​(μ1/2)>12​CP​(μ0)+12​CP​(μ1).\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{1/2})}>\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{0})}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{C_{P}(\mu_{1})}. (A.1)
Proof.

Step 1: The square-shear counterexample. Let

Ω=(−π2,π2)2⊆ℝ2,S=(0110),Bs=(1ss1),νs=(Bs)#mΩ.\begin{gathered}\Omega=\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2},\qquad S=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix},\\ B_{s}=\begin{pmatrix}1&s\\ s&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\nu_{s}=(B_{s})_{\#}m_{\Omega}.\end{gathered}

CP​(νs)−1=λ⁡(s):=infu∈H1​(Ω)∖{0}∫Ωu​d​mΩ=0∫Ω⟨Bs−2∇u,∇u⟩dmΩ∫Ωu2​d​mΩ.C_{P}(\nu_{s})^{-1}=\lambda(s):=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}u\in H^{1}(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}\\ \int_{\Omega}u\,\mathrm{d}m_{\Omega}=0\end{subarray}}\frac{\int_{\Omega}\left\langle B_{s}^{-2}\nabla u,\nabla u\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}m_{\Omega}}{\int_{\Omega}u^{2}\,\mathrm{d}m_{\Omega}}. (A.2)

Note that S2=IS^{2}=I and

Bs−2=I−2​s​S+3​s2​I+O⁡(s3),s→0+.B_{s}^{-2}=I-2sS+3s^{2}I+O(s^{3}),\qquad s\rightarrow 0^{+}. (A.3)

Consequently, for u,v∈H1​(Ω)u,v\in H^{1}(\Omega),

∫Ω⟨Bs−2∇u,∇v⟩dmΩ=∫Ω⟨∇u,∇v⟩dmΩ\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\left\langle B_{s}^{-2}\nabla u,\nabla v\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}m_{\Omega}=\int_{\Omega}\left\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}m_{\Omega} −2s∫Ω(∂1u∂2v+∂2u∂1v)dmΩ\displaystyle-2s\int_{\Omega}\bigl(\partial_{1}u\,\partial_{2}v+\partial_{2}u\,\partial_{1}v\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}m_{\Omega} (A.4)
+3s2∫Ω⟨∇u,∇v⟩dmΩ+O(s3).\displaystyle+3s^{2}\int_{\Omega}\left\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\right\rangle\,\mathrm{d}m_{\Omega}+O(s^{3}).

The numerator in (A.2) defines a real-analytic family of closed symmetric forms, with common form domain H1​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega) and compact resolvent. We next determine the expansion of λ⁡(s)\lambda(s) as s→0s\rightarrow 0. At s=0s=0, separation of variables shows that the first positive Neumann eigenvalue on Ω\Omega is 11, with eigenspace

E=span⁡{e1,e2},e1​(x,y)=2​sin⁡x,e2​(x,y)=2​sin⁡y,E=\operatorname{span}\{e_{1},e_{2}\},\qquad e_{1}(x,y)=\sqrt{2}\sin x,\qquad e_{2}(x,y)=\sqrt{2}\sin y, (A.5)

and the next eigenvalue is 22. In the orthonormal basis (e1,e2)(e_{1},e_{2}), the restriction to EE of the first-order form in (A.4) has matrix −16S/π2-16S/\pi^{2}. Its two eigenvalues are distinct. The lower one is −16/π2-16/\pi^{2}, with normalized eigenfunction u0=(e1+e2)/2=sin⁡x+sin⁡yu_{0}=(e_{1}+e_{2})/\sqrt{2}=\sin x+\sin y.

Analytic perturbation theory for closed symmetric forms [31, Chapter VII, Section 4.6] therefore gives two analytic eigenvalue branches issuing from the double eigenvalue 11. Because their first derivatives at 00 are distinct, the lower branch is simple for all sufficiently small s>0s>0 and equals λ⁡(s)\lambda(s). Thus

λ⁡(s)=1−16π2​s+β​s2+O⁡(s3),s→0+.\lambda(s)=1-\frac{16}{\pi^{2}}s+\beta s^{2}+O(s^{3}),\qquad s\rightarrow 0^{+}. (A.6)

ϕ0=1,ϕk​(x)={2​sin⁡(k​x),k≥1​ odd,2​cos⁡(k​x),k≥2​ even.\phi_{0}=1,\qquad\phi_{k}(x)=\begin{cases}\sqrt{2}\sin(kx),&k\geq 1\text{ odd},\\ \sqrt{2}\cos(kx),&k\geq 2\text{ even}.\end{cases} (A.7)
